Mr. Speaker, I rise today to present two petitions.

The petitioners call upon the government to enact some laws that will provide fair taxation for Canadians. They call upon the government to deal fairly with average Canadians and with those who are having difficulty making it through a difficult time in Saskatchewan. They want the government to introduce a fair tax system in the country.

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition from a number of farmers in Saskatchewan.
The farmers call upon the government to reinstate oats and give it the same protection under the Canadian

Mr. Speaker, despite the vote taken in the House a week ago today, I would like to present a petition signed by 215 residents of Edmonton, almost all of whom are women, that points out that the choice to bear children or not to bear children is a matter of personal choice, not criminal law.
The petitioners point out that the Canadian Medical Association already has guidelines and regulations in place concerning abortion and that criminal sanctions do nothing to address the reasons why women seek abortions or to reduce the numbers of unwanted pregnancies.
Wherefore, the petitioners call on Parliament to refrain from imposing any criminal sanctions against abortion.
I present this, Mr. Speaker, because I am certain the matter will return to the House.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, it is a pleasure to rise in the House to present a petition signed by Canadians who are opposed to the government's GST proposal.

Your petitioners call upon this House to reject the GST proposal again, as soon as it comes back to the House.

Mr. Speaker, I rise with some pride to present a petition on behalf of over 200 Canadians and others from around the world. They have forwarded a petition pointing out that the city of Revelstoke, as a result of the abandonment of the VIA Rail The Canadian train through the Rocky Mountains, has become truly isolated due both to winter closures as a result of avalanches and the fact that there is no scheduled air service to that community.
They point out that the discontinuance puts more vehicles on the Trans-Canada Highway through Rogers Pass. This highway is already close to capacity in summer months and will require twinning, at great expense to the people of Canada.

They further point out that the discontinuance will deny that community in the province of B.C., revenue from the tourist traffic the passenger train carries.
Mr. Speaker, I point out that in addition to almost 200 signatures from throughout the west Kootenays in British Columbia, there are further signatories from Grey Town, New Zealand; Perth, Australia; Nabari City, Michigan; Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; Washington, D.C.; New York, New York; London, Ontario; Alberta, throughout Saskatchewan; Seattle, Washington; and Portland, Oregon. There is a great demand for this service and the petitioners ask that that rail line through the Rocky Mountains be re-instituted.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, question No. 290 will be answered today:

1.	Is Petro Canada exploring for oil in the Ecuador Amazonian rain forest and, if so, for each oil well (a) what is the composition of the drilling muds, including all additives (b) what were the results of the chemical analyses (i) of the sediments settled out from the drilling muds and the formation water in the sumps (ii) of the formation water pumped into the sumps (iii) after water treatment and release from the sumps (c) were the sediments tested for heavy metals and if so, which ones (d) what was the ph readings and oxygen content of the water released (i) how do these readings compare to baseline studies of streams in the vicinity?
2.	Is a fish impact study being conducted at a well, and if so, when will it be completed?

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Jacob Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Petro-Canada reports as follows:
1. To date, Petro-Canada has drilled two wells in the Oriente Basin in Ecuador. Both of these wellsites were constructed and operated according to industry approved, environmental standards which are accepted internationally.
1. (a)-(b) During the drilling operations at both sites all fluids and drill cuttings were contained in drilling sumps dug into laterite clay and lined with an impermeable plastic liner. The management and testing of the mud system was carried out by a leading international mud service company, according to standards which are among the most stringent in the world.
Routine Proceedings
In some cases, geological formations contain low concentrations of heavy metals. However, analysis of the drilling mud and sumps at both locations show the absence of these metals.
Government standards determine the concentration of chemicals that can be released with the fluid portion of drilling muds from the sump into the surrounding environment. If these fluid components do not meet the necessary standards, the sump is chemically treated to neutralize or precipitate out the offending chemicals. The sump is then dewatered, again according to standards, to prevent site erosion, disturbance of local vegetation and pollution of surface water sources.
Following the dewatering of the sump, the remaining mud and cutting components, contained in the liner, are covered over and the sump is capped and contoured to prevent erosion and invasion of surface water.
The procedures described above, including the sump construction procedures and chemical analyses of the mud, were carried out at both sites. One sump has been closed in and the wellsite restored to facilitate natural revegatation. The other sump remains open and secured as Petro-Canada develops their plans for potential further work at the wellsite. Once these decisions are made and necessary work is conducted, this second sump will be restored.
2. Petro-Canada continues to study natural revegetation as well as fish and water quality in nearby local streams to ensure that the corporation's programs are successful.

speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-26, an Act to amend the Railway Act (grain and flour subsidies), as reported with an amendment from a legislative committee.

speakerposition: subtopic
Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There are seven motions on the Notice Paper for the report stage of Bill C-26, an Act to amend the Railway Act (grain and flour subsidies).
Motions Nos. 1, 3 and 6, standing in the name of the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex, are in order and will be grouped together for the purposes of debate.

The intent of these motions is to continue the charge already provided for in the present or existing legislation, namely, Section 281 of the Railway Act, for another five years.
A vote on Motion No. 1 will be applied to Motions Nos. 3 and 6.
A motion similar to Motion No. 2 was moved, debated and negatived in the legislative committee which considered this bill. The intent of this motion in amendment is to continue a charge presently in the statute law with respect to the ports of Halifax, Saint John and West Saint John. This was the principle and intent of the amendment moved in legislative committee.
Thus, I must say that, pursuant to Standing Order 76(5), this motion cannot be selected.
Motions Nos. 4, 5, and 7, standing in the name of the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, delete Clauses 2, 3 and 4 of the bill. Such motions are in order at this stage of our proceedings and these three motions will be grouped for debate.
A vote on Motion No. 4 will be applied to Motions Nos. 5 and 7.

He said: Mr. Speaker, these amendments at report stage of Bill C-26, the at and east legislation, if passed, will delay the removal of this program until 1995. This will fulfil several objectives. It will allow those organizations which are dependent upon these rail rates to plan rational alternative routes and methods to export grain and flour in order to maintain both an equitable return and their competitiveness in international markets.
This bill, as it stands, would adversely affect both the returns of producers and their international competitiveness. In fact, this has already happened. The benefits of the at and east legislation were withdrawn a year ago. The harvest of wheat will start less than one month from now in Essex County in southwestern Ontario. This has left the Ontario Wheat Growers Marketing Board and, indeed, the wheat producers of Canada in a very difficult position.
The government has chosen to withdraw the legislation without any thought to the circumstances or the difficulties it has imposed upon the producers and the local elevators, and the ability of the Ontario Wheat Producers' Marketing Board to move that product into the market during the year.
June 5, 1990

In the past, the Ontario Wheat Producers' Growers Marketing Board, through its pooling system, would purchase the wheat from the farmers, giving them an initial payment upon delivery at the elevators. It would then store that wheat for a number of months if necessary in Bay Port elevators at Georgian Bay. This would allow them to supply Atlantic Canada with wheat or flour during the winter months when the seaway was frozen up and also to export.
Consequently the elevators at Halifax and the port of Saint John have been adversely affected by this legislation as well. The domino effect or the chain reaction to this withdrawal has vibrated across the eastern prairies and all of eastern Canada.
It is ironic to note that the government is now talking about an alternative program, but it is too late. If it was going to have an alternative program, it should have been in place before the legislation was withdrawn. In the meantime we see elevators being demolished or slated for demolition in the Georgian Bay area in Port McNicoll, Midland, and Owen Sound. While these elevators may have been built a long time ago, the one at Port McNicoll in particular, they are still state of the art in terms of their ability to unload large volumes of grain and load it onto rail cars in very short order.
It is interesting to note that of all the witnesses who appeared before the legislative committee, not one agreed with the withdrawal of the legislation. Yet, when the minister appeared before the committee he stated: "Well, the wheat still moved last year." What was not considered was the fact that it had to move at a price which resulted in a lower price to the producer through the pooling system. This impact, when spread through the whole system, is very large. To top it all off, the government announced that the initial payment prices for wheat for this year at approximately $115 per tonne.
So again, the withdrawal of the legislation has been another kick in the pants to producers who are already down with returns that will not result in a profit on investment, management, and risk. The government is withdrawing it without a full examination of the widespread impact it is going to have on our total Canadian economy.
Once those Bay Port elevators are demolished, they will be gone for all time. Consequently, we have to move very quickly. Delaying the implementation of this bill
Government Orders
until 1995 may put a hold on that demolition and put the legislation back into place to enable us to move our product into export position, particularly to supply the Caribbean market in the winter months. That market has been held by Canada to a large extent for many years.
The Ontario Wheat Board alone moved between 150,000 to 200,000 tonnes under this legislation. That amount of product moving through the Atlantic seaports ensured the viability of those port elevators and also the flour mills.
One of the witnesses pointed out that, without CP Rail's main line which services the Saint John grain elevator, "not only the grain elevator would be finished but also many of the facilities that move product in and out of the port of Saint John".
This is another one of the domino impacts of the withdrawal of the at and east legislation. It will put additional hardships on the port of Saint John. Without the movement of grain through it, it may no longer be a viable port. Port officials pointed out that they intend to mothball their grain elevator. Anyone with any experience at all in the industry will know that an elevator can only stay in mothballs for approximately two to three years before it deteriorates to the point where it is no longer a serviceable working grain elevator.
Consequently, the port authorities are quite correct when they point out that this could very well be the death knell for the port of Saint John which has been exporting wheat for a couple of hundred years.
The port of Halifax and its flour mills are also very upset and concerned about the end of the at and east legislation. With these amendments before us today we are responding to their request to keep it operational, not only to maintain its status as a viable port but on behalf of the flour mills there which produce flour for export as well as domestic use.
Therefore, I am putting forward these amendments to delay the demise of at and east programs until 1995. If the government is sincere about coming up with alternative programs, perhaps this will allow it the opportunity to do that and to undo the damage done by the withdrawal of this legislation in the budget of April, 1989.

June 5, 1990
Government Orders
A tremendous number of jobs have been lost. In addition to those lost in rail transportation, there have been jobs lost in the elevators in the Bay Ports on Georgian Bay, and in Saint John and Halifax. There will also be jobs lost if the flour mills are forced to close.
The United States has indicated its intention to subsidize the export of about 3 million tonnes of flour this year. Their Export Enhancement Program is undermining the price of wheat on the world markets. The price of wheat does not reflect that world supplies are at the lowest level since 1971 to 1973. Yet, we in Canada are having to bear the brunt of that, not only with the lowering of world prices but also as a result of the government withdrawing the programs that made this a viable industry in Atlantic Canada, central Canada, and the eastern prairies.
Therefore, I urge the House to support this amendment to assist the people across Canada and maintain the flows of product that we have been accustomed to in the past.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in favour of this motion. It is clear through the work of the legislative committee on this bill that the government has not done a proper study of the impact of this legislation, it has not looked at what will be the full implications not only for the maritimes but for the whole grain industry in this country.
We had a number of groups before our committee, including the Minister of Transport and representatives from the Department of Transport. It was very clear when they were before this committee that they had not done a full evaluation of the reports that had been in front of them. They said unequivocally, in fact, that there had been no reports that were unfavourable to the government's position.
In fact, as has been said many times before, as early as 1985 the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission put an alternative before this government. It said that the at and east must be changed, that the at and east was not adequate as it was and that there should be some changes, that although the ultimate purpose it was serving was valuable it was actually costing the government too much money. It put a proposal in front of the
government, not once but twice in 1985. Upon asking the departmental representatives what sort of evaluation they had done on it, they admitted that they had taken only a very cursory look at it and in fact they had not even had the courtesy to respond fully to the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission.
The fact is that the removal of this program is going to have some wide implications. That has been very clear. We had Dover Flour Mills before our committee. It is the only flour mill on the Atlantic seaboard. To make things clear, this bill is affecting Dover Flour Mills. Dover Flour Mills has no intention of shutting down. It is a very efficient mill and should be commended for the work it is doing to maintain that mill in Atlantic Canada. But as a result of this bill it has lost a commercial export market. Its domestic market is still doing very well but it has lost a commercial export market. Its profits have been eroding and it does rely on the Halifax elevator remaining open in order for it to remain open.
The loss of the at and east, combined with the loss of the feed freight assistance on mill feeds, has had a major impact on the whole agriculture industry in the maritimes. When the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission was before the committee it highlighted again the fact that it was going to cost Atlantic Canada $27 million and hundreds of jobs and that it was going to have an impact on diversification in the maritimes.
We heard from people in the agricultural industry who indicated that the loss of the Halifax elevator would have a devastating effect on the whole livestock and poultry industry in the maritimes.
The city of Saint John was before the committee and outlined some other concerns. The fact that the Saint John elevator has already closed has cost a number of jobs in that city. The line that was used to haul grain to Saint John is becoming more and more questionable. We in the west have experienced rail line abandonment for some time and the maritimes are now starting to experience that same problem. If that line to Saint John is removed, and it is becoming less viable for the railway, it will have a major impact on the city of Saint John.
The port of Halifax appeared before the committee and expressed similar concerns about the loss of the at and east program and the possible closure of the Halifax elevator.
June 5, 1990

The longshoremen appeared before us. They are very concerned because their workers are losing jobs. They have workers with families who are trying to make ends meet who simply do not have work. It is not because they do not want to work, it is not because they are not ready to work, it is simply because the jobs have disappeared because this government, without thinking, has removed a program and is affecting the livelihood of many people in Atlantic Canada.
The Canadian Wheat Board was before us and said that the loss of the ports of Halifax and Saint John will mean the loss of the only ice-free ports on the Atlantic seaboard. If those ports are lost it could mean the loss of sales. As the representative from the Canadian Wheat Board indicated, countries with warm climates and warm waters do not want to go up the St. Lawrence during the winter to the St. Lawrence River ports because they do not want to deal with the ice. In fact, they like the idea of coming to an ice-free port because they are not used to dealing with ice and they do not want to deal with it. If they have the choice of going to an ice-free port or dealing with the St. Lawrence River, they may well go somewhere else.
The Canadian Wheat Board has expressed that the loss of these ports takes away one marketing element that it uses. As we know, this country needs all the help it can get in marketing grain. The Canadian Wheat Board, which is an institution that has done wonders for the Canadian grain industry needs all the help it can get.
The issue boils down to the elevators at Saint John and Halifax. The question that must be asked is if the government is going to remove this program what is it going to put in its place? It has offered nothing. It did not listen to what the APTC had to say. It has offered nothing to put in its place.
I have found this experience very frustrating because the government, despite being hit over the head with information, ignored it and bullheadedly moved ahead with its agenda, which is not always clear to all Canadians.
One thing that was satisfying was that the work we in the New Democratic Party and others have done on this
Government Orders
bill has forced the government to recognize the devastating impact that this bill is going to have. As a result, it has appointed a study to look at the future viability of the elevators at the ports of Halifax and Saint John.
It is great that the government is concerned about the elevators at Halifax and Saint John. It is too bad that it would not have been interested about 18 months ago and looked at some real alternatives to this program so that today, instead of debating the demise of the elevator at Saint John and the potential closure of the elevator at Halifax, we could be debating the very logical and well thought out proposal put forth by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission. A vast majority in each party in this House would favour that sort of proposal. Instead, the government is being bullheaded and is going ahead without any real thought for the consequences of its action.
It is only the work of members of this party, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission and others, that has forced this government to realize that the passage of this bill will have a devastating impact on regional development. The promotion of agriculture in Atlantic Canada is important to its economy. At least we got the government to recognize that. It is really sad that the Saint John elevator is already closed. By the time this study is finished Halifax may be closed. Everything is in limbo. Everything is up in the air.
I want to remind the government that we have to keep in mind that regional development is an important factor in this country. It has been a factor since Confederation. If the government is not going to consider regional development, if it is going to consider only the bottom line, we are going to have problems in Atlantic Canada, Saskatchewan and other regions of the country that do not have a great population base but are part of this Confederation and deserve the consideration of this government.
In closing, I would like to remind the government that it has a duty to all regions of this country to make sure that there is a fair opportunity for all, to make sure that every Canadian, no matter where he or she may live in this country, has the opportunity to work, to raise a family, to make a living and to live in a way that is satisfactory to all of us in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I also want to contribute to this debate and I am not happy to do so. Frankly, it is a little embarrassing.
I listened very attentively to the remarks of the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex in explaining his amendments. For members on all sides who do not appreciate the history of Bill C-26 and the effect of the amendments, what the hon. member for Lambton- Middlesex said in very even, objective, non-provocative prose is absolutely correct. The member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, who a little younger and a little more partisan, got pejorative. He said things that could excite one and perhaps the facts would cause one to get excited. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise for a few moments this afternoon to address Bill C-26, which would eliminate the at and east grain subsidy.
Some members may wonder why somebody from the mountains of British Columbia is speaking on this subject. Quite frankly, my own area of the Kootenays was brought into Canada by a contract with the people and the Government of Canada at the time of a strong secession movement. The West Kootenays were going to follow the normal flow of our economics and were seriously considering joining with Spokane and Washington state. There was an agreement to build the Crow's Nest railway and to have certain rates apply in order to keep us as a part of this country so that we could make our contribution to this act of political will that was and still is called Canada.
This is not a dissimilar sort of situation. Once again we see this government with its dogmatic theology of the private market that, come hell or high water, is determined to let loose those private economic forces to do what they will regardless of the impact on the regions of this country and the very fabric of this nation.
To briefly explain to anybody who happens to be listening, Bill C-26, the at and east freight assistance program, pays a subsidy to the railways on export grain and flour moving by specified routes through eastern Canadian ports. The rates paid by the shipper have been frozen since 1960 with respect to export grain and 1966 with respect to flour.
At the next stage in this discussion my colleagues in the New Democratic Party will be moving an amendment to this bill to set the freight rates for grain and flour shipments to Halifax and Saint John, New Brunswick at 5 per cent higher than the rate for shipments to Quebec City. This is similar in effect to a proposal made by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission. The idea is reducing the cost of the program while ensuring the ports of Halifax and Saint John remain competitive.
The amendment currently before us on behalf of our colleagues in the Liberal Party is calling for the at and east to be left as is. It puts me in mind of the Liberal attitude to almost everything else around here, which seems to be: "Don't touch a thing, don't make a suggestion, feel no sense of responsibility to do something to bring costs a little more in line, don't have any innovative proposals or compromise proposals, just say

no". That attitude is as unjustifiable in this case as it is in the case of the goods and services tax. If people want to say no, they have some responsibility to come up with some alternatives. My New Democratic Party colleagues will do that later in this debate.
Back in the real world outside this Chamber, just what is happening? Since the at and east subsidy ended on January 31 due to one of the provisions of the bill which ends it retroactively, the grain elevator at Saint John, New Brunswick closed on February 28 with a loss of 90 jobs. The elevator in Halifax is in trouble and may be forced to close. The closure of the Halifax elevator will affect the economy of the Atlantic region in several ways.
First, the Halifax elevator plays a vital role as a grain storage facility. Without it Dover Flour Mills, the only flour mill in Atlantic Canada, would probably be forced to close.
Second, without the Halifax elevator shipping feed grains by lake vessel through the port of Halifax, the only competitive alternative to rail transport, would no longer be available. Based on past experience this would result in an increase in the rail rates for domestic feed grains that livestock and poultry producers in the maritimes depend on.
Third, local breweries will face similar problems as they will no longer be able to use water transport for malt barley.
Closure of the grain elevators alone will result in the loss of 573 jobs at the ports of Halifax and Saint John. In Saint John 90 jobs; Halifax, 483 jobs. Another 250 indirect jobs may be lost as well. The closure of Dover Flour Mills would result in another 45 jobs being lost and the loss of a local market for producers of milling wheat.
Livestock and poultry producers in the maritimes are already at a disadvantage when competing with Ontario and Quebec producers. In the opinion of the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission any feed cost increases could place those industries in jeopardy.
What has been the government's response? In response to political pressure from many sectors, including the New Democratic Party but certainly not solely-a lot of people have been involved, particularly many from

Mr. Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to say a few words at the report stage on Bill C-26, an act to amend the Railway Act.
With regard to the at and east rate, Subsection 281(2) of the Railway Act reads as follows:
(2) For the purpose of encouraging the continued use of the Eastern ports for the export of grain and flour,
(a)	rates for grain moving in bulk for export to any Eastern port from any inland point over any line of a railway company subject to thejurisdiction of Parliament shall be maintained at the level of rates applying on November 30, 1960 to the movement of that grain to Eastern ports; and
(b)	rates on flour moving for export to an Eastern port from any inland point over any line of a railway company subject to the jurisdiction of Parliament shall be maintained at the level of rates applying on September 30, 1966 to the movement of that flour to Eastern ports.
Therefore, we are really talking about grain being maintained at the 1960 level and flour being maintained at the 1966 level. The impact of this is not only on western grain producers shipping to European, Mediterranean, and North African customers. There is also a spin-off advantage for the local grain producers in the Atlantic ports of Saint John and Halifax.
There is an advantage for western producers of grain, wheat and barley, as well as oilseed crops. They are facing a serious drop in income this year. Even with the recent adjustments in net-farm income, Saskatchewan goes from a minus $9 million net-farm income this year to minus $116 million, which is a drop of 87 per cent.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if you, as Speaker, with the very large special allowances provided to Speakers had to suffer an 87 per cent reduction in your income, it would practically destroy the financial and fiscal integrity of
your whole operation, or for that matter, the operation of any other hon. member of the House.
Yet, at a time when farmers in Saskatchewan are facing a loss in net-farm income of 87 per cent in this calendar year, the government is removing its support program of the at and east rate which amounts to some $50 million. It is inconceivable that, at a time when we are facing the most outrageous international trade war between the United States of America and the European Economic Community for those markets for grain around the world, we are reducing our export support programs for grain. In fact, the United States has increased its support programs for exports of wheat and a whole range of agricultural commodities from some $600 million last year to $900 million this year. It is subsidizing wheat sales at the rate of $20 to $40 a ton.
At the same time, we are removing an integral support program for our wheat producers in western Canada to ship grain at the 1960 rate for wheat, barley and oats, and moving that up to the current day rate. The impact will be really tremendous, not only for those producers, but for Atlantic Canada in total and those grain elevators in the Great Lakes ports in the area around Georgian Bay.
Our complaint is that, at a time when we are facing a very serious trade war in agriculture commodities, we are unilaterally disarming. The Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence say that we have to maintain our support and our strength for NATO, although they have not actually done that. Surely, if that is important in a military context, then it is important in a trade context that we do not unilaterally disarm our farmers and our producers of grain at such a time. That is essentially what we have done.
In his 1989 budget, the Minister of Finance removed support programs for Canadian agriculture producers of about $500 million. Some of those budget cuts did not actually trigger in until January 1, 1990. However, the at and east rate, which provided some $50 million of support, was triggered last year. That amount of support and encouragement for export of our chief agriculture exports, wheat and oilseeds, was triggered last year. But that is only one. What has to be understood is that there
June 5, 1990

is a whole range of programs: the at and east rate; a reduction in crop insurance in that 1989 budget of $200 million; a reduction in the rail line rehabilitation program of some $50 million; and a reduction in the gas tax rebate.
What does the gas tax rebate mean? Last week, I was talking to a group of grain producers in the southeastern part of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Some of those producers were talking in terms of a fuel tax rebate loss of some $3,000.
The government talks about its grand schemes of a $500 million program to support western agriculture while it glibly overlooks that one year earlier in April, 1989 it reduced support programs to Canadian farmers by exactly $500 million. Essentially it is refunding, with a grand sweep of the pen, support programs. This at and east rate, Bill C-26, is to implement the reduction the government made in 1989.
I believe that the amendment that the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex has introduced into the House is a good amendment, because the government obviously did not know what it was doing. A few weeks ago, it announced that it was going to put in place a special commission to investigate how to support agriculture because it was removing this support to the grain elevators and the at and east rate to Atlantic Canada. Surely, delaying the removal of this rate for five years would allow the government an opportunity to find out what it is going to do to support agriculture as a result of this ill-conceived project to remove the at and east rate.
I would hope that hon. members, especially on the government side, would look very closely at the hon. member's amendment for the at and east rate, so that it would not be implemented for five years. Perhaps by that time, the government either will be out of office or will know what it is doing with this ill-conceived removal of the at and east rate as proposed under Bill C-26.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to debate Motion No. 1 which would have the effect of delaying this particular action to do away with the at and east rates until April 1, 1995.
This motion makes some sense, given the recent actions by the government in a couple of instances when it has indicated that it is prepared to restudy this issue.
Government Orders
That leaves the impression that the budgetary move to cancel the at and east rates without any discussion has created some problems which the government is apparently now talking about redressing.
For instance, on May 16, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds announced that the federal Department of Agriculture would conduct a study on the future of the grain elevators in the Atlantic region. The study will look at the Halifax elevator, the Saint John elevator, a proposed elevator in Summerside, and how they can be made viable. There is not much point in having such a study, if there is no method or means of getting the grain to those elevators. Therefore, it makes eminent good sense to delay the implementation of this government proposal to cease the movement of grains in that direction and to look at other options.
There have been options put forward by my colleague for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, one of which would have the effect of raising the transport rates from Quebec City further east. This would not have cost the government as much money in subsidizing the rate. It would have saved about $10 million, would have provided an opportunity for Atlantic Canada to get used to slightly higher rates, and very likely would have kept the flour mill now faced with closure in Atlantic Canada in business. It would have kept in business the two terminals that are at risk, the one at Saint John which has announced that it will be closing if the program does not go forward, and the one at Halifax which has a very shaky future now that at and east rates have been discontinued.
The impact of the policy change stretches beyond just terminal operators and the jobs that will be lost there which are quite numerous. We understand that the closure in Saint John which occurred February 28 meant a loss of 90 jobs. There is a possible loss of 483 jobs at the Halifax terminal with the termination of this program. As well, the closure of Dover Flour Mills, which is expected if this program goes into effect, will mean 45 more jobs lost and something in the neighbourhood of 250 indirect jobs in those cities, all due to the closures of these fairly major employers.
Further to the government announcement on May 16, there is the statement by the new Minister of Transport on May 30 when he appeared before the committee. He

June 5, 1990
stated that the alternatives to eliminating at and east rates that were put forward by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission had not yet been studied. The government has taken its initiative, stopped the program without any consultation, and has not even looked at alternatives presented by the region affected.
Mr. Speaker, I see your signal. It is one o'clock. I would like to continue after 3 p.m..

Mr. Speaker, this weekend I had the pleasure of officially opening a job entry program for women of the York region who are presently receiving social assistance but wishing to gain the experience and necessary skills to move into the workforce and be fully contributing members of society.
The program called Alternative Paths for Women is funded by the federal government and operated by Lumbers Cuts of Aurora, helping women in the York region wishing to earn and to learn.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to condemn the attitude of Liberal Senators to Bill C-21 which was to come into force on January 1 this year.
The uncertainty caused by the present deadlock is intolerable. Postponing passage of the unemployment insurance legislation is causing considerable harm and is very costly for Canadians.
I regularly receive complaints from my constituents who would be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits under the provisions of Bill C-21 and who are now in financial difficulty because they must wait until the bill is passed.
Bill C-21 provides that $800 million can be spent on skills training for workers and $600 million on new services such as better maternity leave and unemployment insurance benefits for persons over 65.
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce which represents 170,000 businesses has recommended the immediate passage of this bill.
A recent study indicated that two-thirds of Canadians are in favour of the government's proposal for changes in the unemployment insurance system.

In the energy field, Canadians can do a lot more for their environment. For example, individual Canadians can conserve energy and install more efficient lighting
fixtures. Corporations can do the same and electric utilities can promote conservation among its customers.

Mr. Speaker, Varity Corporation received a $200 million bail-out from the federal and Ontario governments. That assistance was successful, it had a $90 million profit last year, but it seems to have no hesitation about biting the hand that fed it.
Varity executives are now musing about moving the company to the United States, a move that would violate the covenant it signed with the taxpayers of Canada. So what, it has already broken the agreement it made to create and maintain 1,000 permanent jobs in Canada by May 1, 1989. In fact, it is 450 jobs short. The taxpayers can bite back. Under the terms of the covenant, the federal and provincial governments can fine Varity Corporation $30,000 per job that it has failed to create.
I challenge the federal government to levy the fine, collect the money and pay it to the workers who have been laid off or who are about to be laid off at Varity's Kelsey-Hayes subsidiary in Windsor. Better still, use it to save Kelsey-Hayes and save those jobs. It is time that this government showed some teeth.

Mr. Speaker, Hollywood creates heroes. Remember Gary Cooper in The Lou Gehrig Story? But in everyday life disease creates the real heroes. I met one of those everyday heroes last weekend in my riding. His name is Donald Glen.

June 5, 1990
Like the real Lou Gehrig, Mr. Glen has Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, or Lou Gehrig's disease as it is more commonly known. It is a devastating disease of the nervous system which destroys the voluntary muscles. Average life expectancy after diagnosis is 2.5 years.
Hollywood will never make a movie about Donald Glen and that is probably okay by him, but it is important to Mr. Glen that Canadians become aware of this disease so that the chances of beating it are better.
Mr. Speaker, there is no cure because doctors and researchers do not know the cause. Today, on behalf of Donald Glen and others across the country who suffer from ALS, I urge Canadians to contact the ALS society in their community and give their support. With the right team effort, we can pull together and help strike out this disease.

Mr. Speaker, this morning I received a letter which says in part: "I have two beautiful children, I am five and a half months pregnant. I have no job, no income, no future, neither does my husband. How are we supposed to feed our children?"
That letter, like many others I receive, comes from a woman who used to be a fish plant worker until her fish plant closed. Her community, like so many others, is in total collapse because of the situation in the inshore fishery in Newfoundland.
Small fish plants in communities like Picadilly, Rose Blanche, Belleoram, and many others by the dozens have been closed because of the failure of the inshore fishery. This failure has nothing to do with another problem we have been hearing much about in the House, the northern cod stock issue. The Minister of Fisheries will know that his program of aid some weeks ago did not address the situation as it relates to these communities. I call upon him to come
forward with an aid package and do it now while there is still time.

Mr. Speaker, today, I rise to announce that members of the parliamentary ad hoc committee on AIDS will be holding a press conference tomorrow at 1 p.m. at the National Press Theatre to release its report.
The report will include recommendations to the Minister of National Health and Welfare for the upcoming National AIDS Strategy, which will be announced later this month.
Members of Parliament from all three parties, and Senators, have been working on a voluntary, non-partisan basis for over a year to confront one of the most serious global epidemics that we are facing today.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Today is World Environment Day. There can surely be no greater threat to the environment of the world than continued nuclear testing and continued emphasis on nuclear warfare and improving nuclear weapons. In fact, while the cold war is ending, the environmental problems in the north are not, and I speak of the north as the Arctic.

June 5, 1990
Oral Questions
The Soviet Union recently announced that as of 1993 it will re-establish nuclear testing on the Arctic island of Novaya Zemlya. This particular site has been used in the past.
Given the prevailing spirit of co-operation we saw with Mr. Gorbachev's visit last week, and the comments he made about a zone of peace in the Arctic, my question to the minister is this. Could he share with us what the Prime Minister conveyed to Mr. Gorbachev about the Arctic and in particular was a circumpolar treaty on the Arctic discussed with President Gorbachev?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Leader of the New Democratic Party for returning to a question which was raised by her colleague and spokesperson on foreign policy in the recent committee hearings on external affairs.
As a result of those discussions, as I reported to the House a few days ago, I raised the question with Mr. Shevardnadze with respect to the shifting of the emphasis of Soviet testing to the Arctic and expressed Canada's concern about the environmental consequences of that testing. I indicated to him that we were particularly aware of the fragility of the ecology there and wanted to ensure that the co-operation established between Canada and the Soviet Union on Arctic matters could apply to co-operation with respect to testing.
I would be prepared to give a fuller briefing to the hon. member or to her colleague from Winnipeg on those discussions if she desires.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister.
The minister is of course aware that Canada is not the only source of the pollution that is destroying the Arctic. The Soviet Union also produces a great deal of pollution.
Canada has the necessary technology to reduce these dangerous emissions, but technology exports to countries in Eastern Europe are controlled by a NATO treaty that dates back to 1949.
What does the minister intend to do to enable Canada to export this technology to all countries?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, the regulations in question do not apply exclusively to NATO. The arrangement involves NATO members but also other countries like Australia and Japan.
Discussions are now under way to change these regulations in order to provide for a broader exchange of expertise and technological skills with the Soviet Union and other Warsaw Pact members.
This is one of the questions that was discussed when Mr. Gorbachev and Mr. Shevardnadze were here, during their visit. I am informed that it was also discussed in Washington. Tomorrow, I will be in Great Britain, where I hope to have an opportunity to talk to my fellow NATO ministers and find out whether we can make a little more headway on the COCOM system.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly appreciate the minister's comments, because it is clearly madness that the health of Canadian citizens is being affected by pollution which Canadians could assist to reduce in another country except for a military treaty.
I would like to raise as well with the minister low-level flights over Labrador. As we know, according to NATO, the plans to build a base at Goose Bay have been scrapped because of the ending of the cold war. However, fears still exist that these flights will not diminish but increase. In fact figures by officials of the department indicate as much as a doubling.
How does the Secretary of State for External Affairs feel about such increases, in view of his comments a week ago about NATO's forward defence strategy and the need to rethink that strategy?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that question is being considered, as the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party suggests, in the context of general discussions that are occurring within NATO.
I am not sure that the specific question of the pace of low-level flights will come up in the discussions in the next two days. I rather doubt that. However, the general
June 5, 1990

question as to the over-all configuration of NATO and indeed the orientation of NATO will be discussed.
If I may refer briefly to the earliest question posed by the Leader of the New Democratic Party with respect to the north, one of the suggestions that has been made by members of the standing committee is that it would be useful for parliamentarians from Canada and the Soviet Union to meet more regularly to discuss matters of common interest in the north.
I made that proposal to Mr. Shevardnadze who immediately accepted. I hope it will be possible through the intermediary of the standing committee to make arrangements for that kind of practical co-operation by elected representatives of the Canadian and Soviet people.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock the hon. member for Mackenzie had the floor. The hon. member has six minutes remaining.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. At one o'clock I was pointing out some of the effects on various regions of the country and on various sectors of the economy that this move by the government to discontinue the at and east rates to Atlantic Canada is having.
The poultry and dairy industries in the Maritime provinces will no longer have access to as much feed grain and will have to pay a higher price for their feedstuffs, putting those industries at risk in terms of continuing to be competitive. Those commodities produced under supply-management systems are the standby and the backbone of the agricultural community in Atlantic Canada.
As well, the decision has meant the complete writing off of capital investments in two or three major points in the country. The terminal at Port McNicholl has now closed down. That terminal was a very low upkeep kind of facility that did not require a lot of maintenance. There are big, concrete silos that require virtually zero maintenance and that will probably stand for another 50 to 200 years with very little extra investment. The belts that take the grain from the bottoms of those silos have been running for 50 to 60 years without maintenance and appear to be ready to continue for many years to come.
The effect of the decision has been to make this investment worth absolutely zero, in fact less than zero. The owners of the property will now have to blow up the silos, clean off the property, and make it available to use for something else. Doing that takes away a storage facility that could be made available on a surge capacity basis for grain and oilseeds producers in southern Ontario. This option is now closed off and forestalled.
The farmers in Ontario are going to have to spend more money either directly themselves or through the commercial grain handling part of the agricultural supply chain. They are going to have some new investments in storage capacity for grains and oilseeds in southern Ontario.
Similarly, in Saint John, New Brunswick, there will be no more grain storage silos left in a few years. There is
no reason for those terminals to exist any more, and they will probably be tom down as well. Again, this takes away any further option of moving grain, other than through the St. Lawrence system. In fact, it makes it more difficult to even out the flow of feed grains and flour grade wheat to the maritime region because it will reduce the amount of storage available.
While the intention is not to close the storage facility at Halifax immediately, the future of that terminal is very much in jeopardy with this decision.
The final effect is that not only are western grain producers losing another shipping option that has been available to them, but the users are going to have to change their pattern of operation. Some of them are going to be forced completely out of business, even though their facilities are good for another 50 to 200 years. The whole thing makes very little economic sense.
The government would have been well disposed to have negotiated a different arrangement such as that suggested by my hon. friend from Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. He proposed adding 5 per cent to the freight rates from Quebec City on to the maritime region. This would permit the traffic to flow on a need and called for basis. This would have permitted the continuation of hundreds of jobs and lessened the negative impact on the agricultural production sectors in maritime Canada. It would have veiy likely kept the flour mill in that part of the region in operation as well.
In closing, I urge the government to reconsider its move to close down the at and east rates at the end of the last crop year. Instead, I urge it to permit the program to continue until April 1, 1995, as this motion requires, so that there can be adequate time for the kinds of studies that the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds are now saying should have been done.

Mr. Speaker, we all know that today we are continuing to participate in a parliamentary charade.
The legislation that we have been debating here has been in effect since last July. We have gone through first and second reading. We have called in witnesses at great expense. We are going through report stage now. We will
June 5, 1990

go through third reading tomorrow. The bill will be sent to the Senate. There will be Royal Assent and proclamation. We are going through the motions to legitimize a government action, which has no legitimate reason to be in a policy, that has been in effect since last July. That is supporting a parliamentary dictatorship. We are trying to expose what the government is doing to the Canadian people.
The elevator at the port of Saint John has been closed because of this legislation. The work force at the elevator in the port of Halifax has been severely reduced. Already we have 1,000 jobs lost in the Atlantic area.
The chairman of the transport committee, even though he is sympathetic to what we are saying on this side of the House, will have no effect on changing the government's mind regarding the withdrawal of this bill.
The amendments of the hon. member for Lambton- Middlesex are a valiant attempt to make a disastrous bill a little better. The government will railroad this bill through without amendments. As a matter of fact, it has already announced a study into the effects of the bill, a bill which has been in effect for almost a year. This is totally unbelievable. The government has implemented a policy and has now announced it will study the effects of the legislation. It will end up re-implementing a very similar program to the at and east grain and flour subsidy after destroying it.
The government already knows the disastrous effects the bill will have on Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, but, it will kill the bill anyway and then re-implement a similar program. The reasons for the policy in the first place have not changed. What was the purpose of the at and east grain and flour policy?
I would like to quote from a witness at the legislative committee from the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission as to the purpose of the flour and grain subsidy:
The "At and East" Grain and Flour Subsidy program was implemented in the mid-1960s to ensure that eastern Canadian ports could compete with United States east coast ports; and to enable the Ports of Halifax and Saint John to compete with the St. Lawrence River ports.
Government Orders
The reason for the subsidy has changed somewhat in that eastern Canadian ports can now compete with the United States ports. The second reason for the program, to enable the ports of Halifax and Saint John to compete with the St. Lawrence ports, is still in effect. The fact is that the Atlantic ports of Saint John and Halifax cannot compete. To the detriment of Halifax and Saint John, the ports in Quebec City, Baie Comeau, and other St. Lawrence River ports will benefit at the expense of Atlantic Canada.
I would also like to refer to the minister who implemented that at and east program, the Hon. J. W. Pickers-gill. In 1966, referring to the reasons for the at and east program, he said: "According to the Board of Transport Commissioners these rates are already unremuner-ative-We decided to keep those rates at their present level and to pay compensation for doing so. This is because we feel there is an equal obligation in this field to the obligation with regard to the Crowsnest. The purpose of this is to ensure that we will have rates which will provide some inducement and incentive to shippers to use the facilities of the Atlantic ports".
Basically, these are the reasons why the minister, Mr. Pickersgill, implemented the program. He viewed it as an equal obligation to the western program of Crowsnest.
In 1975, the program was extended to include the Ontario wheat growers. This was for the purpose of storing grain in the Georgian Bay area and then shipping in the winter, once prices had stabilized, to the export ports in the east. As the board states in their objectives in using this program:
The At and East has allowed the board to put in place an effective
and orderly marketing process.
There was an additional reason for this program and it was that it created an efficient marketing program for the wheat growers of Ontario.
The abolition of the at and east program will severely hurt Atlantic Canada. I would like to refer to some statements that Mr. Keith Russell, executive director of the Atlantic Farmers Council, has made to the legislative committee. Mr. Russell represents about 80 per cent of all farmers in the Atlantic provinces, in that the federations of agriculture from Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland are repre-

Government Orders
sented by this co-ordinating body which they call the Atlantic Fanners Council.
According to Mr. Russell, the livestock and poultry industries in Atlantic Canada require about one million tonnes of grain per year. The Atlantic provinces are growing about half that requirement, that is about
500.000	tonnes. That means they are importing about
500.000	tonnes from western Canada.
At the same time they are not allowed to even investigate-I suppose they could investigate-but they are not allowed to purchase grain from the European Common Market or from the eastern United States, because in order to do so, one needs a licence from the Canadian Wheat Board and it refused to give one. We are caught in a position where we have to buy our grain from western Canada and from Ontario and we are going to have to buy it at a much increased price. Because of the increased cost, it is going to detrimentally affect our livestock and poultry producers in Atlantic Canada.
The main beneficiaries of this program, in addition to Atlantic Canadians, are the wheat and grain producers of western Canada and Ontario. This program is now costing farmers an additional $25 to $30 a tonne in transportation costs of grain coming into the region. This is going to have the effect, according to Mr. Russell, of cutting the number of livestock and poultry growers in half. If this is not going to be a disaster to the Atlantic provinces, then I do not know what it is going to take to show this government that this bill is a piece of ill-advised legislation.
In conclusion, I implore the government, on behalf of the livestock and poultiy producers of Atlantic Canada, to withdraw this bill or at least to agree with the member for Lambton-Middlesex to not implement this program for at least a five-year period so the farmers of Atlantic Canada will have an opportunity to make adjustments to the withdrawal of the program.

speakeroldname: Mr. Howard Crosby (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if you would allow me a few moments to respond to at least some of the comments and statements that have been made in support of this particular amendment and the other amendments proposed to Bill C-26.
I do not think it is too much to say that the amendments are virtually and entirely without merit. I say this for historic reasons. We have heard many times in this debate that the subsidization embodied in the at and east rate was created in the early sixties and affirmed in 1966 as a provision of the Railway Act of Canada. The purpose of the subsidization was to ensure the flow of grain and grain products, including flour, to the east and particularly to the east coast ports of Halifax and Saint John.
Simply on the passage of time and the changes that have taken place over the past 25 years, the subsidy requires some form of re-examination. This re-examination did not start yesterday, it started in 1984 when the government reviewed all the expenditures that were part of the massive deficit that the previous Liberal government had incurred over the years and piled into a $200 billion national debt. I do not think anybody would ever fault the government for reviewing each and every item of federal expenditure.
Of course, subsidies were one of the items that came under review. The question was asked as to whether this form of subsidization was accomplishing a useful purpose, bearing in mind the cost to the treasury that exceeded, in some years, $40 million and was capped in one particular year at $40 million. It is understandable that the subsidy was reviewed and found at fault. This review took place in the mid-80s and the at and east subsidization program was under attack from 1985 onward.
The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission recognized that fact and came forward in 1985, making some suggestions for change. It knew that the at and east subsidy was not fulfilling its purpose, was not cost effective and was not producing all the results that effective government assistance can produce.
All these matters were considered by officials, whether letters were answered or not does not matter. The matter was on the table, it was fully considered, but no positive recommendations were made. No authoritative body, provincial government, railway company, shipping company, or elevator company came forward and said, "Here is exactly what we want to replace the at and
June 5, 1990

east". So a decision was taken in April of 1989 to cancel the at and east subsidy.
That decision was taken in the budget and the legislation embodied in Bill C-26 simply implements a budget decision taken in April of 1989. And here we are, years later almost, debating what is a fait accompli. The members opposite knew in April of 1989 that the at and east had been abolished. They know that in July of the same year, transportation of grain through the system embodied in the at and east rates stopped. They know that all subsidies terminated in January of 1990. They know that grain is not now flowing eastward as a result of the at and east subsidy. They know the game is over. They know fini has been written to the book and now it is time to write a new book on grain movements to the east coast. Now the time has come-
Like what?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
And so the member for Regina-Lums-den, who is not involved in the port of Halifax nor in the port of Saint John, says, "Like what?". Well, now what do you do? Do you start writing a new program before you have terminated the old? Can you have two kinds of subsidies arguably in effect? No, what you have to do is terminate the subsidies and then take the positive attitude toward what might be an appropriate replacement.
You have to listen to organizations like the Halifax-Dartmouth Port Development Commission which has suggested unit trains and are conducting a study to determine whether unit trains can be used to carry grain from western Canada directly to the ports of Halifax and Saint John.
Look at those kinds of suggestions and examine them carefully, not sit in the House of Commons and use arcane arguments to support a policy which has already been eliminated. What, indeed, is the purpose of that? Do they really think they are helping the longshoremen in the port of Halifax? Do they really think they are helping the operators of the grain elevator in the port of Halifax? Do they really think they are helping Dover Flour Mills, by arguing against a matter that has already been clearly established and is now a matter of history? What is the point of that? Are members of the House of Commons, allegedly acting in the interests of the people involved, the people of Nova Scotia, the people of New
Government Orders
Brunswick, the people of Atlantic Canada, simply going to stall this bill so that no resolution of the problem will ever occur?
Is that your purpose? Is that what you want to do for the people of Atlantic Canada? Or do you want to get to work and find replacement policies and programs that will mitigate any damage caused by the elimination of the at and east subsidy? Is that too much to ask members from Saskatchewan to do? Is that too much to ask of members from Ontario? Is it too much to ask members from Nova Scotia to put aside the political rhetoric, and to recognize that a decision has been taken by government and that decision is part of history and to go on to resolve the problem? Is that too much to ask? Is that what they enjoy?
Is it their purpose in life to sit here and involve themselves in useless political rhetoric when there are people at work in the country trying to resolve the problems? They want help from members of Parliament. They want support, but I do not know anybody who appeared before the legislative committee who said: "Preserve the at and east." Since 1985, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission has admitted that the at and east rate is ineffective and that we must move to some other form of assistance.
The members from the New Democratic Party say: "We agree with the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission. We support their submissions." They say: "Keep the at and east and then we will see what else we can get." That is not going to work. They know it. They are just taking political advantage. They think somebody in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick might be listening to them and actually believe that they are acting in their interests instead of putting roadblocks in the way of the resolution of the problem.
I have lived in the port of Halifax all my life. My grandfather served in the House of Commons before me. I do not think anybody can doubt my motives in trying to assist the port of Halifax. Yet, they come here from Regina, Saskatchewan and say: "No, no. Don't eliminate the at and east. Keep it in force. Let's go on for another six days. Cany it over the summer. Don't solve it until the fall." How is that going to put in any alternate programs of the kind recommended by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission? How are we going to act upon any of their suggestions unless we

June 5, 1990
Government Orders
deal with and finalize this matter here in the House of Commons?
I appeal to members to put aside the rhetoric and the partisan, infantile policies. Let us get the bill passed. This will allow us to go on in a positive way to implement some of the recommendations of the Halifax-Dartmouth Port Development Commissions and some of the recommendations that flow from the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission. It will allow us to look at the possibility of unitrains and the cost factors involved, to preserve the elevator, to implement the study that has been undertaken by the Minister of Agriculture and the task force to see if we can preserve the grain elevator, to help the longshoremen and the employees in the port of Halifax to gain other employment.
They do not want to listen to you people. They want jobs. They want the grain elevator operating. They do not want to listen to you. They want some hope for the future and you are not giving them any while debating this bill and stalling it in the House of Commons. I wish my colleague from the city of Dartmouth was here to argue against me and to tell me that the people in the port of Halifax want the at and east rate stalled in the House of Commons.
They want this matter decided. They want to go on. They want hope for the future. They do not want your empty rhetoric any more.

Mr. Speaker, I wish I lived in Halifax so I could run against the hon. member.
In all the years I have been here, I have never heard a member betray his own region and his own city with the kind of garbage to which I have just had to listen. The hon. gentleman forgets that something like the at and east freight rates affect us all from Moose Jaw to Halifax. From where do you think you get that high quality milling wheat? From where do you think you get that high quality feed grain?
Do you think it grew up in the middle of the St. Lawrence River? You do not know a damn thing about grain and grain movement. You do not know anything about it. The hon. member talks about jobs. This bill has already put over 100 people out of work. He talks about making jobs. The hon. gentleman submits that they are
going to replace this. Well, the one thing you do not do, if you are any kind of a government with a handful of brains, is cancel a program until a replacement one is agreed to and ready to put in place. These guys have got nothing.
The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission has made proposals which the government has refused to accept. When we get to Motion No. 2, which is a proposal of the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission, I wonder where the hon. member will be. He will be out behind the curtain, hiding. He will not have the courage to vote for his own city and his own port.
We will support Motion No. 1 of my colleague the Liberal critic because, if nothing else, passing this motion would give the government time to come up with its replacement program that the hon. member for Halifax just talked about. Obviously the hon. member and the government do not have a replacement program. That will give the government a year or two, as long as they are going to last, to come up with their replacement program. They have not got one yet and they will not listen to the people from the Atlantic provinces who have made proposals which the government refuses to act on or even listen to.
The worst tragedy of all is that this is a total emasculation of the parliamentary process. I know Mr. Speaker ruled on the question of privilege of my colleague, the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. He ruled under the rules of Parliament that the legislation was in order. Mr. Speaker frankly said that he did not want to rule on a constitutional matter, that that was to be dealt with in some other place. The problem is, Mr. Speaker, who has the money to go to the Federal Court and then the Supreme Court? I do not, and I doubt if the Standing Committee on Transport can get a budget for it.
In any case, what has happened has happened before and the Federal Court threw the government out of court. The government had to fork over $100 million in storage payments to the Canadian Wheat Board. Why? Because the government tried to make legislation retroactive. That was a Liberal government. This government is doing exactly the same thing. It is giving legislative effect to a bill that has not even passed Parliament. If

that does not violate a parliamentary democracy and violate our Constitution, I do not know what does.
No self-respecting democratic institution should allow the government of the day, any government of any political stripe at whatever level, to bring into legislative effect and legislative force legislation that has not been dealt with and passed by Parliament and received the signature of the Governor General.
This law has been in effect and enforced since July
1989.	The least the government could do is say that the law does not take effect until the day of Royal Assent, and then it would be doing the right thing in terms of parliamentary process.
This amendment gives the government some time. It can keep this at and east rates legislation in effect for a year. If it has an alternative program, fine, bring it in and the legislation to cover it and then repeal the at and east rates. Instead of that, the government just repeals it. It is perfectly understandable why it is done that way. The government does not want to spend any more money. It has no intention of bringing in a replacement bill.
We have moved an amendment, which we will discuss a little later, that implements a request of the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission. The government will not listen to them. The government has heard them but they did not listen, and for the amount of money that the government thinks it is going to save, it is going to end up costing the Government of Canada more money by the cancellation of this program.
It is going to cost the government in lost jobs, lost income, and lost income tax. It is going to cost it in the lack of a grain handling facility in Saint John, which does not do much for Canada's export position, whether it is for flour or grain. It is likely going to cost it most, if not all, of the operation of the grain terminal in Halifax. Then the hon. member for Halifax states that these people want jobs. Of course they do, so why is he supporting a bill that does away with their jobs? Where does the hon. member for Halifax stand on the jobs that the people in his city want when this legislation is causing them to lose their jobs?
If and when the Dover Flour Mill shuts down, that will decrease our export capacity of flour. More significantly, the feed grain users in Atlantic Canada depend on that terminal to store the feed grain.
Government Orders
The hon. member for Halifax talked about unit trains. I do not know where he has been. The issue of unit trains from Thunder Bay to Atlantic Canada has been studied ad nauseam every year since I have been here, and the costs are pretty high. The government of those days and the government of today does not want to spend any more money and ergo unit trains are not being used. They should be in the winter months. In the summer months we can use the Seaway.
The hon. member is talking about using unit trains. What would you do with 100 cars at 2,000 bushels per car, 100 tonnes per car, and a 100 car unit train that arrives in Saint John? Where are you going to put it? The grain terminal is closed. It arrives in Halifax, where are you going to put it? The aftermath of this legislation means forget about unit trains. Dover Flour Mill will have to bring in just sufficient flour or milling grain to see them through month by month. That is about as much as they can store.
It is going to be a jerk-water operation. It hurts the shippers of malting barley. It hurts the brewery industry. It hurts the shippers of malting barley in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. It hurts the shippers of high grade, high protein milling wheat. It decreases our export capacity and capabilities. We lose what we used to have, a flour and feed grain market in Cuba. Cuba sent sugar and rum to the Soviet Union, and the Soviet Union paid us in cash. It was a neat three-way deal. It was in place for about 18 or 20 years. That is down the drain.
There is the whole Caribbean and central American region that is there for us, and what do these guys do? They scrap it. They scrap what we do have, and goodness knows it is little enough.
I do not understand any self-respecting member from Atlantic Canada from any party supporting this legislation. It passes beyond all understanding. I suspect that any member from Atlantic Canada who supports this legislation and all the implications there are to it will rue the day. I can tell them one thing: Do not be a Tory candidate in my part of Canada. You will have to answer for this one, as well as a number of others.
