speakeroldname: Mr. Rod Laporte (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 4
That Bill C-26 be amended by deleting Clause 2.
Motion No. 5
That Bill C-26 be amended by deleting Clause 3.
Motion No. 7
That Bill C-26 be amended by deleting Clause 4.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise to debate those motions. I note that Motion No. 2 was ruled out of order as it had been dealt with substantially in committee. However, the purpose of the motion was to introduce the option that had been put forward by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission, the proposal that has been discussed many times in this House.
I would like to turn for a moment to another area. In fact, the effect of the motions would be to kill the bill and leave the status quo. There is another area that has only been touched on briefly with respect to this issue, and that is with respect to the transportation system in this country generally.
It has been asked a number of times in this House why the government persists in pushing this legislation through. It is clear on the face of the bill and all the evidence that has come forth from the committee and through the House that this bill makes no sense.
However, it does make sense in terms of the government's over-all agenda. It is a private agenda, an agenda that has not been discussed openly, but it is there and it can be seen if one looks very closely. That agenda that the government is coming forth with will change the whole face of agriculture in this country, and it will change the face of the transportation of grain in this country.
The elimination of the at and east grain transportation program is simply a rehearsal for the removal of the Crow benefit that is now being enjoyed by western farmers. It is clear that the government is determined to completely dismantle the grain transportation system in this country as we now know it. The elimination of the at and east program is only one item on the government's agenda in its plan to dismantle our grain transportation system and to reintroduce the Crow debate.
This fall we are going to be into the real Crow debate. This is simply, as has been determined before, a miniCrow debate. We had a Crow debate in the early 1980s. Many members who are here today, my senior colleagues, were part of that debate and did an admirable job with respect to that. That is the issue that is in front of us. What we are facing is the whole dismantling of the way we transport grain, the way agriculture survives in this country and the way it is progressing.
There is no consideration for the survival of the family farm. There is no consideration for the survival of the economic regions of this country. There is simply a concern for bottom-line economics which is coming forth.
This Toiy government is very good at tactics and strategy. It has a strategy and it is putting it forth step by step. It was very clear in part of this bill the strategy that was taking place. It is a strategy that is very concerning. What was happening is that some of the members on the committee were falling into that trap.
The hon. member for Halifax stated in committee that if this subsidy goes it is unfair to the maritimes, because the western farmer still has the Crow benefits, still has the Western Grains Transportation Act and the benefits under it. She said that if the maritimes lose the at and east why should western Canadians keep the Crow benefit? That is a dangerous trap. That is the trap that
June 5, 1990

this government wants people to fall into, the talk of the so-called level playing field.
That is not the case. The reason that we have those benefits in the first place, the reason that we have had the Crow rate and now the Crow benefit, and the reason that we have had the at and east program was to allow the regions of this country to develop. That was the purpose of it.
They are removing the Crow benefit. That is not going to help the terminal at Halifax. It is not going to help the terminal at Saint John. It is not going to help agriculture in the maritimes.
When grain is shipped through Halifax and Saint John, it already gets the benefit of the Crow benefit because that benefit applies to Thunder Bay. Grain for export goes from the prairies to Thunder Bay, and then from there on through Halifax and Saint John. The at and east was simply another program to encourage the use of the elevators at Saint John and Halifax. Now that the at and east program is gone those elevators are in deep trouble. We have seen that one has already closed, and the elevator at Halifax is also in a shaky position.
If the Crow benefit goes, that is not going to benefit the maritime farmer. It is simply going to hurt further the average producer, the average family farm in Saskatchewan, in Manitoba, in Alberta, and in parts of British Columbia. What this government has done is laid the groundwork for the removal of the Crow benefit. It is laying a foundation. It is laying a trap which some people are walking into and which we must be very careful that we do not fall into.
If this Confederation means anything to us, if this country means anything to us-and there is a lot of debate about that these days-we have to pay attention to the regions. There are regions that do not have the same advantages as other regions.
We in Saskatchewan know what it is like to live in a province that does not have some of the economic advantages of other provinces. Certainly under a Toiy government, which we have suffered for the last eight years, we now are a have-not province. We know what it is like to be from a region such as the maritimes because we are experiencing that situation now. This is a government that is not planning to better our lot in life. It is not planning to help the average Canadian. This is a bottom
Government Orders
line economic government that is simply wanting to cut the deficit. It is simply looking after the interests of corporations.
What we have had since the Second World War is a de facto agricultural policy that has seen the family farm struggle. It has seen rural Canada disintegrating. Right now we have a severe crisis in rural Canada. Many of the same problems that exist in rural Nova Scotia are exactly the same problems that exist in rural Saskatchewan. The only difference in some cases is that the economic base is different. In some parts of rural Nova Scotia and the rural maritimes, fishing is the economic base and the same is true in Newfoundland, whereas in Saskatchewan the economic base primarily is agriculture.
The fundamental issue that we have to keep in mind-and I remind members to keep it in mind-is that this government has a strategy. It is a strategy that is going to be turning full force in the fall on to the western producers. We will be having a major change in transportation policy. We will be having a major change in support programs for the western farmer and a whole new attitude toward agriculture. I feel very concerned about that. I feel very concerned for the future of my province, for the future of western Canada, for the future of the maritimes, and for the future of Newfoundland. Bypassing this legislation the government is simply laying the groundwork.
I call upon members to do what they can to keep the issue alive and to show the government up for what it is doing. The government knows that this is its plan and does not hide it. One can see that it exists. It is there to be looked at.
In conclusion, I would remind members that we are simply beginning the debate. This a mini-Crow debate. The real Crow debate will begin in the fall when the government finishes its work on the transportation system and the movement of grain in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I say to my friend for Fraser Valley East that I was here this morning, as was he, at which time I was speaking in support of three amendments put forward by my colleague from Lambton-Middlesex. Now I am delighted to rise and support a set of amendments put

June 5, 1990
Government Orders
forward by the gentleman from Moose Jaw-Lake Centre.
I am surprised the amendments got by the Chair because the effect of the amendments, without telling the Chair how to do its job, as I understand it, would be to negate the bill effectively. There is another way to do that, simply by voting against the bill, but we will not be choosey on this side of the House. If we can beat some sense into the government by whatever means, we intend to do it.
That brings me to what I thought was a courageous move earlier today by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants, a gentleman who is normally in support of the government. He is a Conservative. He has run and been elected many times under the Conservative banner. He and I disagree on many issues, and that is as much to his credit as it is to mine, I am sure. However I do not want to talk about our differences today. What I want to do is salute him and the courage he exercised earlier today. I am sure he will follow through with a vote against the bill later on today.
The gentleman from Annapolis Valley-Hants, although he bears the same party label as those who have sponsored this bill, although he is normally a supporter of the Conservative government in this Chamber, gave notice today-and it took courage; I congratulate him- that he would be voting effectively against the government in this measure which is now before the House.
By way of contrast to what the gentleman from Annapolis Valley-Hants did, it is instructive to recall what the gentleman from Halifax West did, he who has stevedores, longshoremen, elevator operators, and other people in the dozens in the port of Halifax who are his constituents. We have in the one case a gentleman from Annapolis Valley-Hants who does not have very many constituents whose livelihood is directly at stake, although in fairness to him he does have some farmers whose feed prices will be adversely affected if this bill goes through.
Once the beef prices go up.
I do not know how much they are going to go up. Did I suggest to the gentleman that I knew how much they were going to go up?
Nobody was suggesting that you know what you are talking about.

The gentleman from Macleod shows signs of stirring and having some interest in this particular matter. We welcome him to the debate. It is by far his best contribution to a debate during this entire session.
I say to both friends opposite that I do not know in dollars and cents terms how much will be the difference. I know that the impact will be adverse. One does not have to be terribly bright to figure that out. The impact will be adverse.
I also listened to the representatives of those farmers and those grain elevator operators who came before the committee during committee stage. One only has to read the transcripts of the committee hearings, which I have done, to find that people like Mr. Keith Russell, Executive Director of the Atlantic Farmers Council, told the committee as recently as May 17 when this bill was before it that there is a fair degree of concern among farmers in Atlantic Canada about this matter.
I was anticipating the next question as to why it is that I from what is essentially a fishing constituency am standing here right now talking about an issue that is essentially a farm and transportation issue. There is a very simple answer to that question.
While it is true that almost every one of the 151 communities that make up the riding of Burin-St. George's have an involvement in the fishery and are currently being devastated by the downturn in the fishery both inshore and offshore, it is also true that there are three important farming pockets in the riding of Burin- St. George's.
There is the very fertile Codroy Valley. Those of you who have gone to Newfoundland by Port aux Basques will be aware that after getting off the ferry in Port aux Basques and driving the Trans-Canada Highway across the island, within 20 miles of leaving Port aux Basques you will pass on your left particularly, but on your right as well, the very fertile and very picturesque Codroy Valley. It has a farm community which has thrived over the-years and which will be hurt by the obvious increase in feed prices to be triggered by the bill now before the House should it pass.
June 5, 1990

There is a second pocket of farmers a little farther up the highway in what we know as the Robinson's area: the communities of Robinson's, McKays, Jeffries and so on. There is a third pocket on the Burin Peninsula centred around the community of Winterland.
Just a little footnote here for the benefit of my good friend from Macleod: between 1934 and 1949, during that 15-year interregnum there was no elected government in Newfoundland. The democratic government, a Tory government by the way, which had been elected in 1932 suspended itself and in effect voted itself out of office. That must have been the one and only time that a Tory government ever did that. It invited in a British appointed Commission of Government to run things. A governor plus six commissioners were appointed by the British government, three Britishers by birth, three Newfoundlanders by birth, plus the governor who was normally a Britisher by birth.
That seven-member commission was the government for a 15-year period, known as the Commission of Government. It did a lot of clumsy things, a lot of inefficient things, and a lot of undemocratic things. One of the better things that the Commission of Government did during that period was to encourage farming in Newfoundland, in particular to set up a number of farm communities for returning veterans, people who had come back from the Second World War. One such community was Winterland in my riding of Burin-St. George's, as well as some others.
Do I understand that my time is so soon running out, Mr. Speaker? There are many more things I would like to say about these particular amendments. In my digression I wanted to talk about the particular import of this bill to the farm community in Newfoundland, the three pockets in my riding, as well as other farm pockets not in my riding but elsewhere in Newfoundland.
Since time is running out, let me say in conclusion that we are against this particular bill and we are going to try and defeat it in any way we can. We believe that by voting for the amendments of the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre we can send a signal that we are
Government Orders
against the principle and the substance of this bill. I intend to do that.
I believe the gentleman from Fraser Valley East is almost persuaded he ought to do likewise. If so, that will be to his credit, unlike the gentleman from Halifax West who not only betrayed the workers in his riding who are depending on this at and east, but never had the courage to stay in the House and register his vote at the end of the discussion.

Mr. Speaker, I am just going to take a few minutes. I think the member for Halifax West made an attempt to defend himself in the eyes of his own constituents. In the process, he attempted to make it seem that the benefit of this bill is not for Halifax and the east coast but for inland Canada and for the prairies. While there is some benefit as far as western Canada is concerned, the amount of grain that we ship through Halifax and Saint John is minuscule compared to the over-all shipment of grain.
The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission, regardless of what the minister has attempted to put before us, made a number of attempts to have the government hold off on this bill until a number of problems have been solved. The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission is not a fly-by-night group. It is a well established and respected organization representing a cross-section of Atlantic Canada and its transportation needs.
It pointed out in its presentation to the government and the committee that the total identifiable cost of the elimination of these particular rates in the form of wages paid to the people of the community is something over $34 million. They consider this to be a fairly conservative estimate.
Furthermore, it recognized the considerable spin-off activity in the community relative to the at and east rates. This bill will result in the elimination of a source of economic activity for Halifax and Saint John, as well as a source of materials of feed and grain that has allowed them to make use of Canadian products.
These motions, if passed, would keep the bill in place, since it appears the government is intent on eliminating these rates. This would give the commission an opportunity to see what must be done before this bill is put into

June 5, 1990

effect. It has made a somewhat ridiculous suggestion considering that we want to make Canada secure in food products and that Canada buys Canadian products as much as possible. speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT INDOOR AIR QUALITY
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT INDOOR AIR QUALITY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should implement a national strategy for reducing the threats posed by exposure to contaminants in the air indoors that would include a national research centre, technology development programs, a set of national standards on indoor air quality and an information campaign designed to raise awareness of and provide advice on indoor air contaminants.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this afternoon to present this motion on indoor air quality.
June 5, 1990



This is an issue of which many Canadian citizens are acutely aware because of the effect it has on their personal health. I do not think any incident could better give people the understanding of how important the issue of the indoor environment is than the story of the events that transpired in Pennsylvania in 1976.
At that time there was a retired air force captain, Ray Brennan, who was 61 years old. He had been retired for a few years and was having a few heart problems, but he was a keen Legionnaire. He was the bookkeeper for American Legion No. 42 in Towanda, Pennsylvania. As his sister said, all he lived for was to go to Legion conventions.
He set off for Philadelphia in July 1976 to attend a state Legion convention, an affair which typically consisted of lots of good times for people who had fought in foreign wars. He came home a bit tired, his sister recalled, and three days later he had chest pains, a fever, and some difficulty breathing. His sister said he did not want to go to the hospital. "We had to fight him all the way", she said. That very night, with his lungs filling with blood, Brennan died of an apparent heart attack.
That was July 26, 1976. Brennan was the first. Three days later in Clearfield, Pennsylvania, Legionnaire Frank Aveni, 60 years olds, died in much the same way. So did three other Pennsylvanian veterans. On Sunday, August 1, there were six more ranging in age from 39 years to 82 years scattered in towns all around the state of Pennsylvania. All of them had just one thing in common. They had all attended the Legion convention held in Philadelphia from July 21 to July 24, 1976. All of them came down with the same signs and symptoms: headaches, chest pains, high fevers, and lung congestion.
It seemed as though the terror spread without any rhyme or reason. Charles Seidel, an 82-year old World War I veteran from Reading, Pennsylvania, died. People in Williamstown were surprised when John Ralph, 41 years old, suddenly died. People did not want to go to his funeral for fear that they were going to catch something.
Then all of a sudden it seemed to level off. There were no instances of victims passing on this disease to any of their families or friends, so the initial fears of some kind of rampaging epidemic were quelled. In the end, 34
Private Members' Business
people who had attended the Legion convention in Philadelphia in July 1976 died.
As we all now know, they died of what has become known as legionnaire's disease. A bacterium, now called legionella, was the cause. The transmission of that disease is still not completely understood, but we do know that it is caused by inhalation, not consumption, of small particles of contaminated water or even soil. If you were to drink contaminated fluid it would not affect you, but if you inhale little particles of it it could.
The story of the tragic events that unfolded in 1976 in Pennsylvania where legionnaire's disease first occurred highlights as well as anything the fact that the indoor environment is intricately connected with the health and well-being of people who live, work, visit conventions, and do all of the things that are a part of normal modem life indoors.
The motion that I propose is that the government implement a national strategy for reducing the threats posed by exposure to contaminants in indoor air. This strategy would include a national research centre, technology development programs, a set of national standards on indoor air quality, and an information campaign designed to raise awareness and to provide advice on indoor air contamination.
We do not have to look to the United States or further afield than Canada to find examples of important, well-known government programs to deal with indoor air problems. The most recent one in the federal experience was the program a few years ago that assisted homeowners who removed urea formaldehyde foam insulation from their homes. It was a program that the Government of Canada assisted in to ensure that money was available to people who had to incur the cost of removing this foam from their walls and buildings because it was believed that improperly installed the foam insulation was causing health problems in people who lived in close proximity to it.
The fact is that North Americans spend over 90 per cent of their time indoors, either at home, school, or work as well as inside recreation and transportation facilities. Some people have estimated that in Canada this figure is as high as 98 per cent because of our more inclement climate.

Private Members' Business
Prompted by the energy crisis, construction techniques have tended to focus on airtight buildings with a dependence on mechanical ventilation systems. There has been a tendency to view the operation of ventilation systems solely in the context of economic efficiency, that is cutting energy costs, and rightly so.
However, more and more people are becoming aware of the untoward health effects that living and working in these airtight energy efficient buildings can have on them, either because of the lack of ventilation or some of the construction or paint materials that surround them all the time.
More and more consumer and office products are made up with a complex array of synthetic chemicals. These products include the furniture that we use and sit on, the paint on the walls, and the materials that are used in insulation.
We now have for the first time something known as the sick building syndrome. It is the term that is being used to describe large outbreaks of a whole range of illnesses that occur from irritations of the eyes, nose and throat, to major respiratory problems and even in some cases cancers. These health problems ultimately contribute to productivity loss in the workplace and greater allergic sensitivity in the home and in the workplace. In the case of some indoor pollutants, long-term physical impairment can result.
People who live in the national capital region, particularly those who are employed by the federal government, are well aware of the problems that have occurred at the building complex within sight of here across the river at Terrasses de la Chaudiere in Hull, Quebec, known affectionately in English by those who work there as Terrasses de la Shoddy-Air.
This huge new building was leased in the late 1970s by the federal government. Complaints began almost as soon as people began to occupy that building. Unions and researchers indicated that 97 per cent of the workers in that building reported a deterioration in their general health since they had been located there. Some 54 per cent reported more fatigue, 46 per cent experienced frequent headaches, and 43 per cent reported chronic dryness of the nose and throat.
In 1981 about 300 employees of a Ford of Canada assembly plant took sick after returning to work after a nine-day shutdown of the plant. Pumps for fluids used to
cool machines were shut off when the plant closed and bacteria in the coolant had multiplied during the shutdown and spread through the air when the machines started up again.
This is similar to the problem that was ultimately identified as the cause of legionnaire's disease in Philadelphia where the ventilation system connected to the air conditioning system was the source, through the contaminated water that was around it, of the spread of the legionella bacterium among the people who were attending that convention.
The Public Service Alliance of Canada has identified a number of buildings in different places in Canada as problem buildings where their members are frequently experiencing problems related to the sick building syndrome including Terrasses de la Chaudiere, the Portage IV complex, the Harry Hayes Building in Calgary, the Taxation Centre in Winnipeg, and the RCMP buildings in Comer Brook. My staff complain in the West Block on Parliament Hill from time to time.
These are problems that surround us. They are common, everyday problems that workers in Canada are dealing with. They are health problems. They directly affect the productivity of our workers, and they are meritorious of the urgent attention of the Government of Canada.
What are some of the causes of the pollution? One that is of very great importance is radon. Radon, as I am sure you know, Mr. Speaker, is a colourless, odourless gas that occurs naturally. It occurs through the deterioration of natural materials. It causes no problem at all in very low quantities but when it gets trapped in a building problems can be significant. In fact, it is believed that it is second only to cigarette smoking as a cause of lung cancer, with some estimates being as high as 5 per cent to 20 per cent of lung cancer being caused by radon being trapped within residential buildings because they are not properly sealed.
There is a series of concerns about biological contaminants. There is carbon monoxide which at low levels causes fatigue and headaches in healthy people. It can cause chest pains in people with heart conditions and can be fatal at high doses.
There is nitrogen dioxide which results from various kinds of heaters and unvented gas stoves. There are problems of organic gases often resulting from paint, paint strippers, solvents, aerosol sprays and so on which result in eye, nose and throat irritations. They can result
June 5, 1990

in loss of co-ordination, damage to liver and other very serious ailments.
There is formaldehyde, which results from pressed wood products, and UFFI, as well as environmental tobacco smoke, asbestos and lead. These are all common, everyday materials that we know about and hear about which are causing problems for the people of Canada in their places of residence and work.
I suggest that the time has come in Canada to address these problems in an organized and concentrated fashion. That is why I have suggested that by way of a national strategy the government take on a number of initiatives. I do not think these involve great direct expenditure of public money, but I do think that there will be direct benefit to the economy of Canada if we address these problems. Benefit will be realized through increased productivity in the workplace and increased job and worker satisfaction.
It is also important that we recognize the interrelationship of so many aspects of our lives, that we begin to realize that environmental problems exist at all levels. Global environmental problems, of course, concern us all. In fact, the ability of mankind to survive depends on addressing some of those important issues.
Recognizing the importance of integrating mankind with the environment in which we live is also of great importance, whether that is the natural outdoors environment or the indoors environment. It is also important, as a matter of health policy, that we not merely look to find cures for ailments but rather that we look repeatedly to the causes of ailments to see whether we cannot remove some of those. Some of them require us to address these important environmental issues.
The federal government is already involved in some of these issues through the National Research Council which devises the building standards for Canada, through CMHC and through involvement, as the largest employer in Canada, with its employees and the unions that represent them. So I suggest that it would not be too much for the government to co-ordinate, through a national research centre on indoor environmental issues, the research that is currently being done in the federal government; to put together a set of technology development programs; to devise national standards on indoor
Business of the House
air quality and to begin to raise the awareness of people of the importance of these problems and help individuals, employers and building owners to understand how they can contribute to the solutions to the problems that are created by indoor air contamination.
Therefore I propose that the government implement a national strategy to reduce the threats from exposure to contaminants in the air indoors.
I believe that this is a very important health problem for all Canadians, and that as a matter of health policy, all governments, not only the federal government but also the provincial governments, must take an interest in these problems and find solutions to the medical problems caused by environmental factors indoors.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House draws attention to a very important national issue which concerns all Canadians. Whether we are in the home or the workplace, the quality of the air we breathe has a direct impact on our health. With our cold climate and the time that we spend indoors we could say that indoor air quality is very much a Canadian concern.
The importance of programs related to this cannot be over-estimated. Over and above the health concerns there is the enormous economic aspect of this issue. There is convincing evidence that employers can enhance the productivity of their employees by providing them with a well-designed and ventilated workplace.
Efforts to address this challenge on a national scale are certainly vital and the government recognizes this fact. The hon. member's motion is seriously flawed in that he ignores and downplays the important work that is already underway and the major contribution that is already being made by scientists and engineers across Canada.
Many government departments and agencies, as well as private sector institutions, are working together on
this problem. There are clear responsibilities and recognized leadership roles, and I would like to speak specifically about the National Research Council of Canada. I feel that the motion is a swipe at the NRC and the work of the people at the NRC's Institute for Research and Construction. By calling for the creation of a national research centre and technology development programs, the member shows that he may not be fully aware of all of the programs and the role that is already being played in this field.
In fact, the NRC's Institute for Research and Construction already is the national research centre for the Canadian construction industry. NRC engineers, scientists, architects and technologists at the institute pool their professional talents to develop cost-effective technology for safe, durable construction.
An important part of this work is related to indoor air quality. The institute helps building owners and managers across the country address ventilation and air quality problems through new engineering systems and other technologies related to employee safety and comfort. IRC also performs its own research to improve ventilation as a means of achieving good indoor air quality in projects of benefit both in the home and the workplace and it is specifically concerned with airtight construction techniques.
As we all know, airtight construction measures can save energy but they also create indoor air quality problems and magnify the effects of emissions from new construction materials. Last year, for example, the institute's researchers made important strides in this field by developing reliable procedures for studying the airflow patterns in apartment buildings. This work will help engineers and scientists identify air leakage characteristics of buildings and this, in turn, helps in defining the ventilation needs of newly constructed buildings.
The institute is working with the Canadian Home Builders' Association in this and other work and it is thus truly linked to the national effort. An example of the national scope of this work is a recent NRC collaboration with the Home Builders' Association to survey the airtightness of hundreds of homes across the country. This survey and other studies will help define the need for mechanical ventilation systems in homes.
June 5, 1990

In the future the NRC institute will be developing computer models and other information systems to help transfer technology about physical and human performance associated with indoor air quality. This information will be made available to building operators in all parts of Canada to use as design guidelines that link the physical attributes of space to its intended use.
This work is definitely tied into a national strategy as it and all of the Institute for Research and Construction is overseen by the nationally representative Canadian Construction Research Board. This board includes the leaders of the construction industry and the unions as well as public sector executives from the provincial and federal departments and agencies and universities with an interest in this field.
Furthermore, the NRC, under the terms of its act, has an important national leadership role in all areas of national construction standards as it is responsible for the development of the national building fire codes. The NRC's national codes are praised world-wide and reflect the state of the art in construction regulation.
The code development process is reviewed for its consultative approach which involves over 300 volunteers across Canada. The institute's employees are working constantly with the code committees and with the provinces and territories to harmonize regulations across this country and to help ensure quality construction techniques on national standards.
The success of the institute's approach to the national public building codes has been recognized in many awards and citations. Last year, for example, the prestigious Royal Bank Award was presented to Dr. Robert Leggett, the first director of the NRC's division of building research and the man who guided the code process for more than 20 years. Clearly, we have a well established and widely supported system for setting national building standards that does not need to be duplicated or undermined by a new one.
The hon. member's motion also advocates a national information campaign. He is clearly unaware of the efforts being made by the NRC and the Institute for Research and Construction to make technology transfer a part of all research programs. For over 25 years the NRC has been presenting an across Canada seminar series called Building Science Insight. Last year, for example, about 1,400 professionals in 14 cities attended
Private Members' Business
that conference. In these seminars, technical experts provide authoritative answers to a host of issues such as material selection, design details and maintenance practices.
The institute also spreads information about its research through hundreds of scientific papers and reports as well as in newsletters distributed across the country through the regional chapters of the Canadian Construction Research Board. The institute also spreads the word about the latest building technologies through its key role in scientific and technical training. An increasing number of young researchers are learning their trade with NRC. They then take their knowledge of the latest technologies in indoor air quality and other areas with them to careers in industry and government.
Information on air quality techniques and other new building technologies are also passed on through NRC's construction technology advisory network.
Thirty-six advisers, with about 700 years experience in total, serve clients across the country. The advisers help local building industries through technical advice and guidance on the evaluation procedures of NRC's Canadian Construction Materials Centre. They also help firms access NRC's vast store of technical expertise and even arrange support for air quality research and other projects under the NRC's Industrial Research Assistance Program.
In conclusion, I would like to commend the hon. member for his desire to draw attention to the indoor air quality issue and for his support of scientific and technical approaches to the problem. However, I believe that we should not ignore the tremendous contribution already being made in this field. There are excellent programs under way at Health and Welfare Canada, CMHC, private sector institutions, and the National Research Council's Institute for Research in Construction.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to engage in the debate today. I want to congratulate my colleague from Ottawa South for bringing this motion forward.
The subject of indoor air quality, whether at home, in the industrial workplace, in aircraft, or in any other area, is one that is topical. It has been for some years and, as

June 5, 1990
Private Members' Business
yet, has received rather scant attention from government and industry.
In 1981, May Britt Carlson, who was the labour attache to the Swedish embassy, travelled for years from one end of Canada to the other addressing labour, schools, workshops, and senior public servants from departments of labour and departments of health in various provincial jurisdictions. She tried at that time to draw attention to the major problems being created and the major health risks caused by poor indoor air quality, particularly in offices and in industry across Canada and around the world.
While there has been some research and there have been some laws passed, and some enforcement, the degree of concern necessary to do something serious about the problem of indoor air quality in Canada has left a lot to be desired.
The motion before us, and I will read it into the record, states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should implement a national strategy for reducing the threats posed by exposure to contaminants in the air indoors that would include a national research centre, technology development programs, a set of national standards on indoor air quality and an information campaign designed to raise awareness of and provide advice on indoor air contaminants.
It is a worthwhile motion. I am glad it is here and hope it is not talked out. It will serve a major purpose in helping to focus attention on the problems of inadequate laws and particularly inadequate enforcement.
While the intent is proper and laudable, there is a problem in the attitude, and that is an attitude prevalent in almost all law-making institutions in Canada. It is kind of a legal mind-set that, if we change the law or educate ourselves, then something will happen. It is my experience, and the experience of literally millions of Canadians in industrial workplaces across Canada, that no matter what laws one has and no matter how much education one has, if you do not have enforcement mechanisms-whether they be public enforcement or self-enforcement-in the work place, then nothing worthwhile is going to be done.
I want to give an example of this. I will not take my limited time to illustrate all the kinds of sickness hazards that exist due to poor indoor air quality. I think those are
well known. They can be looked up by anyone with an interest.
I want to refer to one classic example in my own province of British Columbia that shows how a vague law can be much more worthwhile than a law that spells out everything. What is important is that the government has the political will to see that something actually gets done in the workplace and in homes where it matters to people.
In the late 1960s, some of us in the B.C. forest industry discovered a dilapidated old copy of something called the Factories Act. This was legislation stemming from the early 1930s. About all it had to say about air quality was that the air should be clean and that there should be a healthy work environment. It lacked any specificity at all. Because of that and as soon as we had a government that was prepared to act-unfortunately it was there only from 1972 to 1975-suddenly we had major clean-ups in factories all over British Columbia without a sentence of law being changed.
I want to say exactly what the situation was. We had this law on the books. When we phoned Victoria in the late 1960s, no department of government could tell us which department was responsible for the legislation or who had to enforce it. Later when we-the NDP-went into government, we found out when the government changed that there were only two people in the entire province on staff to enforce that law. They were supposed to inspect annually every factory-old and new- and every industrial undertaking in the province before it opened. We asked them: "How did you do this job?"
They said: "We did telephone book inspections." We asked: "Do you mean to say you just phoned companies and asked them if they were in compliance with the law?" They answered: "No, we did not have time to do that. We just wrote the names in the telephone books into our annual reports." That was a classic case of lack of political will. We did not change an item in that legislation. Because we had inspectors in every region of the province that co-operated with both labour and management and went around the work sites, we had major clean-ups far more than anybody had ever dreamed, and without compulsion.
Even if we could pass this motion, there has been a total lack of political will evidenced on the other side of the House. It is six years, almost to the day, since Bill C-45 was passed to look after the occupational health and safety interests of employees of the House of

Commons. Part III would set up joint health and safety committees with some teeth and influence in this place so that we could clean up the problems in the Wellington and Confederation Buildings having to do with asbestos.
People are working in asbestos and do not know it. They do not know what to do about it when they do find it, and nobody makes them do anything about it even when it is discovered. This government has simply refused to proclaim Part III which it, we, and the Liberal Party all passed almost six years ago to the day. That shows the kind of lack of political will there is here.
While I support wholeheartedly the motion of my colleague from Ottawa South, until we get a government with some political will, I doubt that it will do much good. I think the hon. member for Ottawa South will probably agree with me when I point out that we do not even need a new national research centre. I think the member would probably agree that the Canadian Centre of Occupational Health and Safety might be a good place from which to start.
After a great deal of pressure from this side of the House both from our party and the Liberal Party, the government has finally agreed in a half-baked sort of way to do what it can to keep the centre limping along at least until the next election. That is the hope of all of us. By giving them this job to do we could not only have some excellent expertise readily available, but we could give that institution a new lease on life by giving it another major project that they already have some experience in to be able to conduct some work on behalf of all of us.
I said that I was not going to comment in detail on many of the specific problems, but I would like to urge all hon. members and anyone in the public who is interested in the air quality in their homes, their factories, or their workplaces, to see a Public Service Alliance of Canada film that I attended the premiere of a few months ago on the sick building syndrome. Watching a few minutes of that video would do more to convince all of us how serious these problems really are, not just for our employees or for employees generally, but also for
Private Members' Business
those of us who work or live in buildings that are still not healthy places.
The Public Service Alliance of Canada did a commendable job in producing a film that the layman can understand. Again I urge all members to view it. I will not say any more at this point except to say-and I am not giving any hints to people out there in the workplace-that we know of the sick building syndrome in Ottawa and of some of the towers that we have had here, resulting from the energy crisis and the NEP related laws a few years ago.
Sometimes I think that a sledgehammer through a few windows around this capital would do a lot more to clean up and create a healthy workplace than lobbying for laws and enforcement to get some fresh air into some of these buildings. Better that than wait months and perhaps years more before we finally get a government with the gumption and the nerve actually to do something about its problems.

Mr. Speaker, I am thankful for the opportunity to provide this House with an update on recent and current initiatives undertaken by Health and Welfare Canada to maintain and improve the health of federal government employees. Not the least of these is the department's ongoing investigation and monitoring of indoor air quality in facilities where its employees work. However, experience has shown that problems of indoor air quality often arise in conjuction with other problems in the work environment. And so, before speaking specifically of recent actions connected with indoor air quality control, I think it would be opportune to situate those activities within the broader framework of the department's overall approach to maintaining a healthy workforce. I am certain that the hon. member, given his obvious interest in the health and well-being of public servants, will find the following thumbnail sketch of Health and Welfare's activity in this important area both valuable and informative.
Health and Welfare Canada is fully cognizant of the threat posed to the health of its employees by exposure to contaminants in the air inside office buildings and has, for some time now, been taking countermeasures to ensure against this potential danger. This mission is carried out by the Public Service Health Directorate of the Medical Services Branch, which provides a high

June 5, 1990
Private Members' Business
quality and comprehensive program of occupational and environmental health services to client groups. These services consist of health protection and promotion activities designed to support and enhance the physical, mental and social well-being of clients, and include: environmental and health surveillance that focuses on the health and well-being of the individual and the physical environment where people work; education and health promotion activities aimed at encouraging healthy living and working habits and the reduction of detrimental or hazardous activities in the workplace, at home, and in the community; counselling and employee assistance services to assist, support and enhance the ability of federal public servants to carry out their activities and responsibilities in the workplace in a safe, healthy productive manner; and consultative and advisory services to federal departments concerning the health of employees in the workplace.
The Public Service Health Directorate is responsible for providing these services to federal public servants, people working in federal facilities, residents of Indian communities, the travelling public, V.I.P. visitors to Canada, and in the Yukon Territory, for the provision of environmental health services on behalf of the Yukon Territorial Government. It is also worth mentioning that the Public Service Health Program co-ordinates these activities and services with other departments and agencies of the federal government and other sectors of the Canadian health care system.
The Public Service Health activity maintains an occupational health program for more than 240,000 employees in the Public Service of Canada. Its tasks are to promote occupational health and safety; to provide health services designed to ensure the health and wellbeing of all federal employees, regardless of location; and to minimize the incidence of work-related illness. These tasks are carried out by a variety of professional staff including Environmentel Health Officers, Occupational Health Nurses, Employee Assistance Advisors/ Consultants and licensed physicians. The Public Service Health Program also operates a clinic in Ottawa which is the main vehicle for providing health services to federal employees in the National Capital Region and the foreign service. There is also an Occupational Health Unit which is responsible for the provision of consultative, field and analytical services to regional personnel
concerned with occupational and environmental health programs.
The Employee Assistance Program, which is part of the Public Service Health Program, is designed to help organizations implement procedures to effectively prevent employee problems from affecting their job performance and to create a route whereby employees with a problem are referred to the best professional resource available. In compliance with the Treasury Board policy of 1977, Employee Assistance Services are available at every federal government worksite.
Pre-employment and periodic health examinations are conducted on many occupational groups of federal public servants in order to protect their health and safety, that of their co-workers, and the general public. A major review of this activity, with participation from other federal departments including the Department of National Defence, Corrections Canada and Transport Canada is scheduled for completion in 1990. Among other things, there will be an attempt to replace routine annual examinations with screening examinations tailored to the needs of specific occupational groups.
The Occupational Health Unit of the Public Service Health organization provides analytical and field services which includes special investigations and studies of specific work sites; analysis of data, samples and specimens; remedial recommendations, where appropriate; educational sessions for occupational health staff and employing departments; plus technical support for professional staff in the field. Assistance is also provided to regionally based Environmental Health Officers across the country who deal with environmental conditions and hazards to the health of public servants in the workplace. They provide services which include monitoring, surveillance and educational services to all federal facilities and workplaces.
It is the Environmental Health Officers who carry out investigations of air quality complaints, normally at the request of federal government departments. They can request a stop work order if a serious hazard is found in a public service workplace and will make recommendations to correct the problem or remove the risk. They liaise with other departments and agencies such as Labour Canada, Public Works and Environment Canada. They co-operate in solving problems and exchange professional information about areas of mutual concern.
June 5, 1990

They work closely with departmental managers and health and safety committees.
Having described the program structure by which Health and Welfare Canada carries out its health in the workplace responsibilities, I would now like to mention a few of the more outstanding examples of indoor air contaminants investigations recently carried out, since it is this particular area of this activity that interests the hon. member.
On October 29, 1988, the Department of National Defence closed its Lancaster Park Supply Depot in Edmonton, Alberta, following an epidemic of complaints from employees of stuffiness of the nose, itching and irritation of exposed skin, and soreness of the eyes and throat. An extensive survey was carried out by PSH staff in order to identify the problem and make recommendations to DND officials. Following a survey and examination of employees by occupational health nurses, and physicians, and where necessary, dermatologists, and an environmental survey by Environmental Health Officers, it was recommended that the warehouse air be humidified, avoiding chemical irritants in the atmosphere and that adequate dust control with particular reference to fiberglass be instituted; and that vigilance concerning asbestos be maintained.
A full cleanup operation took place in May, 1989. All staff returned to work and the warehouse is now operational. Further steps were taken to promote the health and well-being of the workforce such as promotions and presentations on lifestyles and health; occupational cancer and diseases associated with asbestos.
No discussion of indoor contaminants would be complete without mentioning tobacco smoke. According to studies done by Health and Welfare for the period 1984-1989, tobacco smoke was identified as a primary culprit in the contamination of indoor air. Until roughly 1987, environmental tobacco smoke was ubiquitous in Canadian federal workplaces, and was accepted by most investigators as a normal constituent of indoor air that did not merit comment in reports. More recently, perceptions of Health and Welfare Canada investigators have changed. By 1987, some of them considered envi-
Private Members' Business
ronmental tobacco smoke to be a significant contaminant. By 1988, for a number of reasons, smoke-free federal workplaces were being seen. On January 1, 1989, a smoking ban in all federal workplaces came into effect.
From what I have said, I think it is obvious that the federal government has been implementing a national strategy for reducing the threats posed by exposure to contaminants in the air indoors. Of course, more can always be done, and this is happening as well. Right now, Health and Welfare Canada is assisting in the financing and promotion of the Fifth International Conference on Indoor Air Quality and Climate: Indoor Air '90, which will take place July 29 to August 3, 1990, in Toronto.

Mr. Speaker, I want to start by thanking my colleague from Ottawa South for his motion and for the non-partisan and thoughtful way in which he has brought to the attention of the House a serious problem that needs to be addressed.
I was concerned to hear the parliamentary secretary refer to some suggestion that perhaps my colleague might have been critical of the NRC in his comments, that he might have been unaware of the work the NRC is doing in this field, and of the efforts being made to make their work available, known and used by building owners and managers throughout the country.
I think the comments were entirely unwarranted. No one who has sat in the House for any period of time and listened to the debates can be unaware that my colleague from Ottawa South has been instrumental in bringing to the attention of the House, the government and the public, the very serious damage being done to the National Research Council and to its contributions to science and technology in this country, and his very strong defence of the role of the National Research Council in all aspects of its work.
One would normally think that when a group of employees move to a new building, and in the case of many public service employees from temporary buildings that had existed from the time of the Second World War, that those employees would be just delighted with their new accommodations, happy to settle in, to have straight

June 5, 1990
Private Members' Business
and even floors for the first time in their working life. In fact, that is not what happened. From the minute certain buildings in the national capital region were opened and occupied, there were persistent and serious complaints from employees about the effects on their health from working in those buildings.
I do not think people moved into those buildings and suddenly starting looking for something to complain about. If anything, at least superficially, their working environment had been substantially improved and normally they would be overjoyed.
It has been a long effort to bring to the attention of employers the problems of the buildings in which they work. I do not intend to repeat the excellent information that has been put before the House by my colleague, but in 1988 the Public Service Alliance of Canada eventually out of frustration went to the point of actually producing a rather thick document for its members. Because the normal process of trying to bring their complaints to the attention of management simply were not being dealt with, they literally put out for their members a manual on how to deal with their complaints, how to identify the problem, how to document those problems and how to get action on those problems.
The manual they put out for their members outlines quite clearly that we are dealing with "sick buildings" and that the effect of working in sick buildings is sick people. The symptoms worsen during the day and as the week progresses and most disappear on the weekend. There has been some tendency on the part of management and government to think that they are dealing with a group of hypochondriacs, and to take these problems less than seriously. I do not think any responsible employer can believe that a group of employees suddenly turn into hypochondriacs overnight. These are very real problems, they are not unknown to the international scientific community and they deserve the very serious attention of government.
As well, people not working for government are subject to the same problems as we try to control our use of energy, make our buildings more airtight and produce a more controlled environment. Apparently we have also produced very sick environments. We seem to be less aware of it in North America. Already in Europe some
governments have made significant progress in determining the causes and solutions to the sick building problem.
My colleague from Ottawa South has brought forward a motion which hopefully will improve our knowledge of this problem, and make us aware that solutions must be found. I am sorry that the government members have decided that this is a bill that should not be voted on because I think it is one that is eminently in the public interest.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to discuss the subject of indoor air quality.
The public has always been concerned with air pollution but until a short time ago the focus was mainly on outdoor air quality and the release a chemicals into the atmosphere. It is now recognized that non-industrial indoor environments can contribute significantly to human exposure to airborne pollutants. The Department of National Health and Welfare has been involved with indoor air quality for at least a decade and remains active in this area.
In 1980, through the federal-provincial Advisory Committee on Environmental and Occupational Health, a working group on indoor air quality was established for which the Department of National Health and Welfare provided support.
In 1987, the Department of National Health and Welfare published, on behalf of the advisory committee, exposure guidelines for residential indoor air quality which presented guidelines and recommendations on 18 substances or groups of substances. To our knowledge, these were the first guidelines on indoor air quality established in any jurisdiction in the world. This year the guidelines have even been expanded to include radon and a new edition is now being published. Work in the department is continuing to identify other contaminants of concern which will be included in future editions of the indoor air quality guidelines.
Also, in 1987, the department published a report entitled Significance of Fungi in Indoor Air-A Report of a Working Group. This document, prepared by a departmental working group, reviewed the emerging issue of moulds and fungi as indoor air pollutants and potential hazards to health.

The current indoor air quality guidelines are restricted to residential buildings. The quality of air in many offices though falls within the responsibility of provincial governments to monitor and regulate. Unfortunately, many of the most conspicuous problems have to do with air quality in non-residential settings, namely offices, schools and public buildings. As a result, a new federal-provincial working group has been formed to investigate these problems.

Mr. Speaker, I asked a number of questions a few months ago now, I think on December 8 in the case of one and January 23 in the case of the other, of the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs and the hon. Minister of Fisheries of the day. My questions concerned the seizure of two Canadian fishing vessels, the Fonzie and the Viscount within Canadian waters on July 5, 1989. Those fishermen were accused by the United States of fishing above what is known as the A-B line, which is the boundary demarcation between Canadian waters on the one hand and Alaskan waters on the other.
The fishermen themselves had the A-B line programmed in their loran, so they were aware that they were fishing in Canadian waters, but in order to avoid a dispute with the American Coast Guard, which had been harassing Canadian fishermen in the area at that time, they steamed south farther into Canadian waters to avoid contact with the United States Coast Guard.
Nine hours later, the U.S. Coast Guard came into Canadian waters, far into Canadian waters in what they
Adjournment Debate
called "hot pursuit", although it could hardly be called "hot pursuit" nine hours after the initial contact with these two fishermen. The Coast Guard steamed into Canadian waters and seized those Canadian fishermen inside Canadian waters.
When the boats were seized, or boarded by the U.S. Coast Guard, the Canadian fishermen contacted External Affairs through the local fisheries officer and were assured that Canada would provide legal assistance to the fishermen. If they simply surrendered to the U.S. Coast Guard, they would get legal assistance afterward.
In fact, they were seized and after their boats were taken to Ketchikan, Alaska, they were unceremoniously thrown out of the United States until their hearing, and these fishermen got absolutely no assistance from this government. In fact, they had difficulty getting the government even to answer their letters concerning the assistance promised by Coast Guard radio.
What a way to treat Canadian fishermen, legally fishing in Canadian waters, doing what Canadian fishermen are permitted to do as a consequence of their licences and their Canadian citizenship.
After the seizure of the boats, the federal government refused to help. It was only after lobbying from the Pacific Trailers Association, the fishing organization that represents the two fishermen on the west coast of British Columbia, and only after representations from members of Parliament in this House and the two questions that I asked, one on December 8 to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and one on January 23 to the Minister of Fisheries, that the government promised some assistance.
The provincial minister responsible for fisheries in British Columbia also came to their assistance. As a result of these combined lobbying efforts, the Minister of Fisheries and the Secretary of State for External Affairs decided to come down with a paltry $25,000 supposedly to help these fishermen pursue their case in Alaska.
Because of the small amount of the aid, these fishermen could not pursue the case and had to drop the case. As a result, they lost a part of their catch and a substantial amount of fishing time. One of the fishermen who lives in my constituency may be forced to give up his house because he mortgaged his house in order to finance his boat, his fishing and also to finance his legal fees. The federal government, although it had promised assistance, never delivered the required amount. As a

June 5, 1990
Adjournment Debate
result, at least one of these fishermen has ended up bankrupt.
The concern that fishermen have on the west coast is that they are wondering if this government is going to defend the right of Canadian fishermen to fish in Canadian waters.
Is this government, having promised to provide legal assistance to fishermen who get into problems with the United States Coast Guard, which is known to harass Canadian fishermen fishing from Canadian vessels inside Canadian waters in order to try to advance their territorial claim in Dixon Entrance south of the A-B line, going to protect those fishermen? To date this government has not shown the backbone or the courage to do that and now many fishermen on the west coast feel that if you want to get protected by the Canadian government when you are fishing legally in Canadian waters, it is probably better to have a United States passport.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I want to thank the hon. member opposite for bringing this forward again in this House. I must say that in listening to his remarks, I could not disagree with him more fully.
Yes, it is true that on July 5 of last year, two Canadian vessels the Fonzie and Viscount were arrested in the Dixon Entrance, one and a quarter miles south of the A-B line in an area that is claimed by Canada and the U.S. It is alleged that they were illegally fishing earlier that day in the undisputed U.S. waters. Both captains deny that they had crossed the boundary into the disputed U.S. waters in Alaska.
At the time of the arrest, the fishermen sought advice from the government. The statements that were made by the Canadian Coast Guard radio led the fishermen to believe that they had received an undertaking from the government for legal assistance.
From the time of the incident, the government has worked continually to persuade the U.S. authorities to drop the charges because the arrests were a violation of an understanding between Canada and the U.S. on mutual restraint in the disputed area. Legal assistance was provided through diplomatic channels and the provision of advice to aid their case. The Canadian Embassy in Washington twice protested the arrests of the Canadian crews and vessels by the U.S. Coast Guard in Dixon Entrance and requested their immediate release and the dropping of charges. The arrests were also protested in Ottawa by the Department of External Affairs to the U.S. Embassy at the level of senior officials.
In addition, Canada's concerns over these incidents were raised repeatedly at bilateral enforcement meetings. During discussions with senior U.S. officials in Ottawa on August 2 and September 25, and again in Washington, D.C., on December 18, we requested that the civil charges against the vessels be dropped. In April of this year, a tentative out of court settlement was reached with the Alaskan government. The agreement should be finalized imminently.
The government provided all forms of legal assistance in this case normally provided to Canadians facing charges outside Canada. Moreover, in view of the exceptional circumstances that existed in this particular case, financial assistance in the amount of $25,000 was provided to the Pacific Trailers Association to contribute to the association's efforts to help the Canadian fishermen operate in the disputed boundary areas off the B.C. coast. These efforts should ensure that fishermen have a better understanding of the legal and enforcement issues in the disputed zone in Dixon Entrance in order to prevent such incidents as occurred last summer.
Newly developed guidelines for fishermen concerning the disputed zone in Dixon Entrance are now available from the department. Guidelines for use by the Canadian Coast Guard concerning boundary incidents will also be finalized shortly.
I want to make it abundantly clear that the Government of Canada is concerned. The A-B line constitutes the international boundary for all purposes in Dixon Entrance and the government is determined to ensure that Canadian fishing vessels have unimpeded access to all Canadian waters, including Dixon Entrance.
In this regard, a public meeting will be held on June 21 in Prince Rupert with fishermen's groups, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the External Affairs officials to discuss issues related to the boundary in Dixon Entrance.

Mr. Speaker, on December 7 of last year, I rose in this House to ask the Prime Minister, in the wake of recent reforms and economic hardships in the Soviet Union, when he was going to help President Gorbachev, give him something tangible to enable him to meet the population's expectations.
My question was responded to by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and with all due respect, I did not receive a satisfactory response. Maybe the Parliamentary Secretary today will give me a better one.
The Prime Minister had recently returned from a trip to the Soviet Union where he claimed that "in terms of bilateral co-operation the visit marked a watershed in Canada-Soviet Union relations. We signed 14 bilateral agreements-more than had been signed in the previous 20 years-on subjects ranging from international affairs to Arctic co-operation, to the environment, to military and cultural co-operation, to investment protection".
Since that day, which was November 27, 1989, as this House knows we have had various visits from Soviet officials, parliamentarians such as today's parliamentary delegation of the Supreme Soviet led by Mr. Rafik Nishanov and most recently, of course, Mr. Gorbachev himself. I have yet to hear any details as to whether there has been any progress or success with respect to these 14 agreements.
I cannot help but feel rather cynical about the intent of the government when it signs such sweeping agreements, all-encompassing agreements, especially in areas where the government's own commitment is highly questionable. Examples would be the agreements on the Arctic and on the environment.
It was brought to our attention in the time leading up to the recent summit on the environment that Canada had made a behind the scenes deal with the United States and Britain to veto a proposal offered by several other countries on the levels of reduction for CFs. Such behaviour truly undermines any effort we may want to make internationally on any given issue. At home we are
Adjournment Debate
not even able to get an already watered down green plan off the ground.
Ideas are great if they are followed by substantive goals and objectives which can be measured by results within time frames by successive re-evaluation, re-examination, revision.
We have the same problem with PCBs in our food chain in the north. Granted, there seems to be a will to do something. The Prime Minister himself on that same day offered an endorsement by President Gorbachev toward co-operation in the Arctic with respect to this very issue, but there is a long distance between endorsing and doing something about it. What guarantees did we get that this would become a priority for the Soviet Union?
We are fast losing any influence that we may have had on events around the world. What Canada says these days is met almost with a polite impatience as we self-importantly and self-righteously condemn or congratulate as we see fit.
When we get assurances from the Foreign Minister of the Soviet Union that medical supplies are reaching and will continue to reach Lithuania, and they do not, we seem surprised and almost shocked, as if we had done something wrong. I am not surprised or shocked, because for the last six years, I and my colleagues on this side of the House have watched this government become merely a shadow and a voice piece for the Government of the United States.
The opportunity to show leadership has risen again. The changing face of eastern Europe and the Soviet Union has presented Canada with a rare chance to take the initiative in the inevitable changing role of NATO.
Yet what do we hear? On the one hand, we hear the Secretaiy of State for External Affairs propose a new direction for NATO by rejecting the policy of maintaining nuclear weapons in Europe. On the other hand, we hear senior External Affairs departmental officials say that Canada continues to support the strategy of maintaining a mix of nuclear and conventional weapons in Europe. I thought it was the politicians who set policy and the bureaucrats were there to administer it. It seems it is the other way around here.
For once I think that the Secretaiy of State for External Affairs is moving in the right direction. The

June 5, 1990
Adjournment Debate
time has come for NATO to take up responsibilities that better represent and better serve the present day realities.
Were NATO to become less threatening by giving up on the traditional argument of nuclear weapons as the ultimate deterrence, we may find the Soviet Union less paranoid of a united Germany and more willing to dismantle its forces, other than as we heard Mr. Gorbachev say when he left the United States that this could lead to another cold war if we insist that the united Germany be a member of NATO.
I truly feel that isolating the United States, Britain and France, the only members of NATO who are developing air-launched nuclear weapons to replace land-based nuclear missiles and artillery, and showing them up as countries with misplaced and outdated policies will serve to further the call from the international community to re-evaluate global priorities.
I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs first to clarify his position-and I hope that his position is that of rejecting current policy-and stick to his proposal during his meeting on June 7 and June 8 of the North Atlantic Council so that we are allowed to play a central role as NATO transforms itself and so that Canada can be free to promote peacekeeping processes, peacekeeping forces, and become truly a nation that can once again make peace a priority as it did under Liberal governments under Pierre Elliott Trudeau, Pearson, St. Laurent, et cetera.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad I am in the House because I think some of the points that have just been mentioned by the hon. member do require a response. I would like to say that I recall his question in this House last December very well. In fact, as reported at page 6612 of Hansard for December 7, 1989, the hon. member stated that the Prime Minister "has just set back the termination of the cold war for another 10 years".
The overstatement and the hyperbole involved in that assessment is unfortunately typical of the strain that is carrying through some of his assessment late this afternoon in his continuing review of the many different facets of what is happening in eastern and central
Europe, the Soviet Union, and the Canadian response to it.
He wound up, with his heart covered, almost with a Liberal Party appeal to the memory of Lester Pearson and Pierre Trudeau and Canadian policy in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union in those days. There is not a person on this planet who does not recognize that there has been a change in the relations in those countries.
We have seen a shift from totalitarianism to democratic regimes. We have seen a shift from the Communist Party domination to multi-party states. We have seen a shift from centrally planned economies to the market economy. We have seen the cold war ending in place of pursuit of collective security and dialogue. The very kind of meeting that was held in this city last week between our Prime Minister and Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev and between our Secretary of State for External Affairs and Foreign Minister Eduard Shevardnadze give clear evidence of the highest attention that is being paid to the continuing evolution of Canadian policy in that region.
The hon. member, as he is his party's critic for External Affairs, has touched many different aspects and issues in his brief remarks, too many to respond to in total right now. However, I would refer him to the excellent discussion and debate which we had in this House last Thursday on the whole question of Canadian foreign policy in eastern Europe. There was a lot that was put on the record, to which I would refer him, at that time showing how in very specific ways the government is continuing to follow up on these agreements that were assigned last November in the Soviet Union. The Prime Minister suggested that the Soviet Union have observer status at GATT. Since the Prime Minister made that suggestion, the GATT has agreed to grant the Soviet Union observer status.
I could go on as I did last Thursday when again then you had to cut me off, Mr. Speaker, but the list is so long of positive action that I commend it to the hon. member for close study.
