Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak again on an issue of very serious concern to the business community of the national capital region, and that is the lack of direct air service from this region to the American midwest. It is having a serious effect on business in this region and on the attempts of our local business community to diversify the
June 5, 1990

economic base, which have met with substantial success, and to become part of the growing market from here to the year 2000 for tourism and conference business.
The business community of Ottawa-Carleton, and of the entire national capital region, are not asking for any preferential treatment. They are simply asking for objective and fair treatment of the government to ensure that they are able to enjoy the kind of access to their markets and to their customers that is enjoyed by virtually every metropolitan region in the country.
The national capital region is the fourth largest urban metropolitan area in Canada, and yet it is the only major urban centre in Canada-the only one-that is discriminated against in this way. Under the bilateral air agreements between Canada and the United States it is the only urban centre specifically denied the right to direct air service to the American mid-west. This situation has existed since 1966 and has been ignored in one subsequent round of negotiations with the Americans on the bilateral air agreement.
The business community has proposed a simple solution. It has documented the need for the service. It has secured the support of American officials for a minor change. It has convinced American Airlines to provide this service on a regular daily basis between the National Capital Region and Chicago, providing access to its markets and customers in the American mid-west. It has documented the harm being done to the local business community because this service is not available.
The solution is quite simple. The service that is now available between Montreal and Chicago can be extended by declaring Ottawa a co-terminal with the Montreal airport. That would allow the airline to simply service Ottawa as well as Montreal as part of the same route.
An even simpler solution has now been proposed to the government by American Airlines and as yet has not been responded to.
Adjournment Debate
I want to address briefly some of the important impacts the lack of this service is having on the business community locally.
First, I want to quote from a letter from the Minister for International Trade, who was then Minister of Transport, to Len Potechin who is now Chairman of the Ottawa Economic Development Corporation and is a past chairman of the Ottawa Carleton Board of Trade. In that letter, the minister agreed that Ottawa should have more international flights and suggested that "the real challenge is to persuade Canadian and foreign airlines that Ottawa is a market worth serving". The minister also states, "It is hoped that business leaders like you will continue to try to attract international visitors to Ottawa, as it is only through traffic demand that international service will be developed".
The local business community did indeed do its homework. It spent substantial time and substantial amounts of money documenting exactly what the minister asked it to do in April, 1987.
I want to put a bit of an historical perspective on this. In the early 1970s, Ottawa as a community and the entire region faced the need to start diversifying its economy and becoming less dependent on the federal government for employment. It did that. It developed a strong and reasonably stable, but still fragile high technology base that has become the core of the high technology industry in Canada. It developed a conference and tourism business and invested in a conference centre specifically to attract international business which is going to be the bulk of tourism business by the year 2000.
It has become the economic hub of eastern Ontario as conjunction with its sister city, Hull, was to western Quebec, an area that is recognized as an economically disadvantaged region not only in Ontario but in Canada.
Now we find that many of our high technology companies, in order to service their clients, are having to establish offices in the United States. It is simply not productive for business people, who could normally take a two hour flight to be at their business destination, to have to leave Ottawa for Toronto in order to reach American markets. We know that Toronto is congested and delays are extensive and frequent because of the over-crowding and the safety measures that have had to be taken at Pearson International to restrict the number

June 5, 1990
Adjournment Debate
of flights landing at any given period of time. These delays have often meant missed flights. As a result, a business trip that could take place in one day often requires an overnight stay, extra expenditure, and extra wear and tear on extremely valuable and talented personnel.
The community has documented the need for this service. It did exactly what the Minister of Transport advised. It had a very extensive survey done. In fact, it used the results of that study to persuade KLM to provide direct regular service to Amsterdam, which is now happening. It used it to persuade Wardair to provide direct and frequent service to Gatwick Airport in London.
The Government of Canada is the only party it is unable to persuade that these studies are valid, the services needed, and would produce economic benefits not only for the urban area but for the entire region, and with respect to the high technology sector, for the entire country.
The community is upset that the government has said to open up trade, to go out and compete and then ties one hand behind their back. It is concerned that in a deregulated atmosphere when it is now dealing with private air companies, it is giving preferential treatment to airlines in Canada, protecting them from competition on a route that they do not want to service.
Why is the government putting the interest of a private airline and its profits ahead of the interests of an entire business community? That is the question the business community of the National Capital Region is asking.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks address the hon. member's question about why the government has not approved the proposal by the Ottawa-Carleton Economic Development Corporation for a new Ottawa-Chicago air service. As was stated in the House on February 19, by the former Minister of Transport, this government has been sensitive to the request but the proposal posed certain difficulties.
Air services between Canada and the United States are governed by bilateral air agreements, particularly the Main Air Services Agreement of 1966 which the member opposite mentioned, last revised in 1974. There is no provision in this agreement for an Ottawa-Chicago service. The inclusion of a provision for an Ottawa-Chicago service in the agreement would require that the agreement be amended to meet the requirements of the National Transportation Act. Amendments normally come about through govemment-to-govemment negotiations.
Therefore, the government cannot unilaterally approve the service in question, even if the proposal made by the Ottawa-Carleton business community contemplates service by an American carrier.
More importantly, Canada prefers a broadly-based pro-competitive approach that seeks to provide efficient air services to all our communities and opportunities for our air carrier industry. This cannot be achieved on the basis of piecemeal negotiations focusing exclusively on the needs of a single community.
When negotiations are undertaken with the United States, they will have to take an account of the national interest, including the aspirations of other Canadian cities that have made representations for improved services, and here I am thinking of Halifax, Edmonton, Calgary, Winnipeg, to name but a few.
Let me assure you that Ottawa's request, along with those of other Canadian communities, has been given serious consideration. The government, however, is not prepared to take actions at this time on behalf of a single community which could jeopardize Canada's ability to pursue a broadly-based re-negotiation of the Canada- U.S. air relationship on terms favourable to Canada and to all interested communities.
